# Dox and the other Dart backends

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/concepts/dart-frameworks/

# Dox and the other Dart backends

This page compares Dox with four other ways to build a backend in Dart: Dart Frog, Serverpod, Shelf (with `shelf_router`) and Alfred.

It lists facts only.
Each project is good at different things.

!!! note "Facts can change"
    The facts about the other projects come from their own docs, READMEs and pub.dev pages, read on 2026-10-22.
    Projects change. Check their docs before you decide.
    Where this page is not sure, the table says "see their docs".

## What each one is for

- **Dox** is a full backend framework, in the style of Laravel. It has routes, controllers, typed DTOs, an ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and a CLI.
- **Dart Frog** is a small backend framework. It is built on Shelf. Routes come from the files in the `routes/` folder.
  It describes itself as "a fast, minimalistic backend framework for Dart".
- **Serverpod** is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server. Serverpod generates a typed Dart client for the Flutter app.
  It has an ORM, auth, streaming and a hosted service (Serverpod Cloud).
- **Shelf** is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework.
  `shelf_router` adds a router. You pick every other part yourself.
- **Alfred** is a small server in the style of Express.js. Routes, middleware, WebSocket and static files are built in.

## Feature table

"Not built in" means the project does not ship it. You can still add a package for it.

| Feature | Dox | Dart Frog | Serverpod | Shelf + shelf_router | Alfred |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Routing | Route classes: `Route.get(...)`, groups, resources, domain routes | Routes from files in `routes/`, dynamic and nested routes | Endpoint classes become typed client methods. A separate web server (Relic) has its own routing. | `Router()` with `<param>` patterns, nested routers | Express-like, `:id:int` params with types or regex |
| Typed request validation | `@Dto` classes, checks generated at build time, `422` with errors | Not in their feature list (see their docs) | Typed, generated parameters for endpoints. Rules: see their docs. | Not built in | Route params only (type or regex) |
| ORM and relations | `dox_orm`: models, has one, has many, belongs to, many to many | Not built in | Built in: filters, joins, one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many | Not built in | Not built in |
| Migrations | `dox migrate` (SQL or Dart files) | Not built in | Built in, versioned migrations | Not built in | Not built in |
| Auth | `dox_auth`: JWT and session guards. Password hashing (`Hash`) is in `dox_core`. | `dart_frog_auth`: Basic, Bearer and Cookie middleware | Built in: email and password, Google, Apple, GitHub, passkeys and more | Not built in | See their docs |
| WebSocket | A Socket.IO v4 server (`dox_socketio`) and raw `Route.websocket` | `dart_frog_web_socket` (`webSocketHandler`) | Streaming methods over a managed WebSocket | `shelf_web_socket` | Built in |
| OpenAPI | Generated OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON, YAML) and a docs page | On their roadmap, not done | See their docs | See their docs | See their docs |
| CLI and code generation | `dox` CLI, `build_runner` for DTOs, models and OpenAPI | `dart_frog` CLI: `create`, `dev` (hot reload), `build` | `serverpod` CLI, generates server and client code | No CLI (`shelf_router_generator` for routes from annotations) | No CLI |
| Native binary | `dox build` makes an AOT binary | `dart_frog build` makes a production build with a Dockerfile | Deploy to Serverpod Cloud, Docker or Terraform. Binary: see their docs. | Your app is plain Dart. Compile it like any Dart program. | Your app is plain Dart. Compile it like any Dart program. |
| Multi-core | One isolate per CPU core by default | See their docs | One isolate per process. Scale with more processes and server roles. | `serve(..., shared: true)` and your own isolates | Yes, a multi-isolate mode is in their README |
| HTTP server | Native server in Rust, also for WebSocket | Shelf on `dart:io` | Relic (their own) for the web server. API server: see their docs. | `dart:io` `HttpServer` (`shelf_io`) | `dart:io` |
| Databases | Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite | Not built in | Postgres, SQLite (also SQLite on the device). Redis for cache. | Not built in | Not built in |
| Code sharing with Flutter | `@Dto` classes in a pure Dart package, see [Share code with Flutter](../guides/share-code-with-flutter.md) | Plain Dart packages. A generated client is marked "in progress" in their feature list. | Generated client package, and shared packages for models | Plain Dart packages | Plain Dart packages |
| License | MIT | MIT | BSD-3 for most packages. The main `serverpod` package is SSPL. | BSD-3-Clause | MIT for the core. Some parts BSD. |
| First release and maturity | New (2026) | First on pub.dev in 2022, 1.0 about three years ago | First on pub.dev in 2021, now 4.x | First on pub.dev in 2014, 1.0 in 2021 | First on pub.dev in 2021, 1.x |
| Maintenance (on 2026-10-22) | Active | Active. Moved to the `dart-frog-dev` group in 2025. Last `dart_frog` release: 1.2.6 (November 2025). | Active. Release 4.0.4 in October 2026. | Active. Published by `tools.dart.dev` (the Dart team). | Last release 1.1.3, about 17 months ago. Unverified uploader. |

Sources (checked on 2026-10-22):

- Dart Frog: [dart-frog.dev](https://dart-frog.dev), [github.com/dart-frog-dev/dart_frog](https://github.com/dart-frog-dev/dart_frog) (docs in `docs/src/content/docs`, the roadmap and "The Future of Dart Frog"), [pub.dev/packages/dart_frog](https://pub.dev/packages/dart_frog)
- Serverpod: [docs.serverpod.dev](https://docs.serverpod.dev), [github.com/serverpod/serverpod](https://github.com/serverpod/serverpod), [github.com/serverpod/serverpod_docs](https://github.com/serverpod/serverpod_docs) (scalability, streaming, shared packages, database connection), [pub.dev/packages/serverpod](https://pub.dev/packages/serverpod)
- Shelf: [pub.dev/packages/shelf](https://pub.dev/packages/shelf), [pub.dev/packages/shelf_router](https://pub.dev/packages/shelf_router), [github.com/dart-lang/shelf](https://github.com/dart-lang/shelf), [`serve` API docs](https://pub.dev/documentation/shelf/latest/shelf_io/serve.html)
- Alfred: [pub.dev/packages/alfred](https://pub.dev/packages/alfred), [github.com/rknell/alfred](https://github.com/rknell/alfred)

## Speed

This page does not compare speed. Dox's own numbers (hello world and a `/db` read) are on [Performance](../digging-deeper/performance.md).
To compare, run the same test on your own machine, with each server on the same number of cores.

## When to pick Dox

- You want a full framework in one place: routes, typed input, ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and OpenAPI docs.
- You know Laravel. See [Coming from Laravel](coming-from-laravel.md).
- You need MySQL or MariaDB, not only Postgres.
- You want typed DTOs with the same rules on the server and in a Dart or Flutter client. See [Share code with Flutter](../guides/share-code-with-flutter.md).
- You want an OpenAPI document made from your code, for clients that are not written in Dart.

## When to pick something else

- **You want a framework with many years of use.** Dart Frog, Serverpod and Shelf have been out for years. Dox is new.
- **You want a hosted service.** Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud. Dox has no hosted service. You deploy it yourself (a binary or Docker).
- **Your app is Flutter only, and you want the client made for you.** Serverpod generates a typed client for every endpoint. Dox does not generate a Dart client. It generates an OpenAPI document.
- **You want a small tool with few parts.** Dart Frog is simpler. You add only what you need.
- **You want to build your own stack.** Shelf gives you the base parts, and the Dart team publishes it.
- **You need features Dox does not have yet**, like events and listeners. See [What Dox does not have yet](status-and-roadmap.md#what-dox-does-not-have-yet).

# Status and roadmap

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/concepts/status-and-roadmap/

# Status and roadmap

This page shows what works in Dox today, what is missing and what is planned.

## Packages

What the states mean:

- **Stable**: works, has tests and has had real use.
- **New**: works and has tests, but it is newer and has had less real use.

All packages follow semantic versioning: a breaking change only comes in a new major version.

The packages in the main repo share one version number. The other packages live in their own repos and have their own version numbers. See [Contribute](../community/contribute.md#packages-in-other-repos).

| Package | What it does | State | Tests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dox_core` | Routes, middleware, controllers, request and response, isolates, config, the IoC container, exception handler, sessions, CSRF, rate limit, security headers, health check, test client | Stable | 528 tests in 61 files. CI runs them on the native server. |
| `dox_orm` | Query builder, models, relations, `whereHas`, scopes, casts, `withCount`, transactions, row locks, many to many writes, polymorphic relations, factories, seeders | Stable | 549 tests in 51 files. CI runs them on Postgres, MariaDB, MySQL 8.4 and SQLite. |
| `dox_validation` | `@Dto` rules, fluent schemas, JSON Schema, Standard Schema | Stable | 149 tests in 8 files |
| `dox_builder` | Code generator for models, DTOs, env classes, the container and OpenAPI | Stable | 86 tests in 5 files |
| `dox_annotation` | Annotations used by the generator | Stable | 6 tests in 1 file. Mostly tested through `dox_builder`. |
| `dox` (CLI) | `dox create`, `dox serve`, `dox build`, `make:*`, `migration:*`, `db:seed`, `queue:*`, `schedule:*`, package commands | Stable | 132 tests in 12 files |
| `dox_migration` | Migrations for Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite | Stable | 36 tests in 5 files. CI runs them on each database. |
| `dox_auth` | JWT and session auth guards and middleware, access tokens you can revoke, gates and policies | Stable | 201 tests in 8 files |
| `dox_cache` | Memory, file and Redis cache, tags, locks | Stable | 94 tests in 4 files, with Redis in CI |
| `dox_storage` | Local disk and S3 (and S3-compatible) storage | Stable | 153 tests in 10 files, with MinIO in CI |
| `dox_openapi` | OpenAPI 3.1 document and a docs page | Stable | 63 tests in 4 files |
| `dox_socketio` | Socket.IO v4 server with a Redis adapter | Stable | 119 tests in 11 files, with Redis and the real `socket.io-client` in CI |
| `dox_queue` | Queues and jobs | New | 96 tests in 12 files, with Postgres, MariaDB and Redis in CI |
| `dox_scheduler` | Run tasks on a schedule | New | 106 tests in 6 files, with Redis in CI |
| [`dox_mcp`](../packages/mcp.md) | MCP server: tools for AI clients over Streamable HTTP, signed sessions | New | 15 tests in 1 file |
| `dox_view` | [Views](../the-basic/views.md): `.dox.html` templates with layouts and components | New | 40 tests in 2 files |
| [`dox_inertia`](../the-basic/inertia.md) | Inertia.js server side: single page apps with React, Vue or Svelte and Dox controllers | New | 34 tests in 2 files |
| `dox_mailer` | Email with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark and sendmail, mailables, Markdown mail, notifications | New | 122 tests in 12 files, with a fake SMTP server |
| `dox_http_native` | Native HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket server in Rust, on the isolate's own thread. Dox has no other server. | New | 65 Dart tests in 4 files, and 32 Rust tests |
| `dox_postgres_native` | Native Postgres client (Rust tokio-postgres), the Postgres driver. Has TLS (`sslmode`, `sslRootCert`). | New | 41 tests in 7 files, plus the `dox_orm` tests |
| `dox_mysql_native` | Native MySQL and MariaDB client (Rust mysql_async), the MySQL driver. Has TLS. | New | 30 tests in 2 files, plus the `dox_orm` tests |

`Hash` (bcrypt password hashing) is in `dox_core`.

!!! note "About test coverage"
    The repos do not measure line coverage. Counts are `test(` calls in each package's `test/` folder.
    A test inside a loop counts once, so `dart test` can report more tests.
    The CI setup of the main repo is in `.github/workflows/test.yaml`. The packages in their own repos have their own CI.

## What Dox does not have yet

| Feature | Status | What to do today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Events and listeners | Not there | Model events are there. See [Model events](../database/model/events.md). |
| Password reset | Not there | Make a signed, short-lived token, send it with [Mail](../digging-deeper/mail.md) and check it in a controller. |
| Localization | Partly | Validation messages can follow the request locale (`req.locale`). There is no general translation helper. Keep your own message maps. |

## Planned

### Later

- Localization

The package CHANGELOGs have an `Unreleased` section when changes wait for the next version.

## How to help

- Try Dox and open an issue when something breaks or is missing.
- Pick an item above and open an issue first, so the design can be discussed.
- See [Contribute](../community/contribute.md) to set up the repo and run the tests.

# Contribute

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/community/contribute/

# Contribute

This page shows how to work on Dox: set up the repo, run the tests, release packages and update the docs.

To send a change, fork the repo and open a pull request.

## Setting up local development

### 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:dartondox/dox.git
```

### 2. Install melos

The repo is a [Dart pub workspace](https://dart.dev/tools/pub/workspaces).
The melos config is in the root `pubspec.yaml` (under `melos:`). Use Dart 3.13 or newer.

```bash
dart pub global activate melos
```

### 3. Run melos bootstrap

It runs one `dart pub get` at the root. All local packages are linked.
There is one `pubspec.lock` for the whole repo.

```bash
melos bs
```

### 4. Useful commands

```bash
# Run all tests.
# Use `melos run test`. `melos test` is a built-in melos command.
melos run test

# Analyze and check format (same as CI)
melos run analyze
melos run format_check
```

### If the project does not run

1. Remove `pubspec.lock` and `.dart_tool` at the root.
2. Remove any old `pubspec_overrides.yaml` and `pubspec.lock` in `packages/*` (left from melos 3).
3. Run `melos bs` again.

## Release (maintainers)

The `Release` GitHub workflow (`.github/workflows/publish.yaml`) publishes all public packages to pub.dev.
It runs when you push a tag like `v<version>`.
It uses pub.dev automated publishing, so it needs no token or secret.

### Steps

The full guide is [RELEASING.md](https://github.com/dartondox/dox/blob/main/RELEASING.md) in the repo. In short:

1. Set the new version in the root `pubspec.yaml`. Then run `bin/update_versions.sh`: it sets this version in every package.
   Close the `## Unreleased` section of each `CHANGELOG.md`.
2. Merge the release PR, then push the tag `v<version>`. This publishes to pub.dev.
3. Release the matching `dox-sample` template.

The native packages (`dox_http_native`, `dox_postgres_native`, `dox_mysql_native`) are not in this repo.
See [Native packages](#native-packages) below.
`dox_orm`, `dox_migration`, `dox_socketio`, `dox_storage`, `dox_queue`, `dox_scheduler`, `dox_inertia`, `dox_view` and `dox_mailer` are not in this repo either.
See [Packages in other repos](#packages-in-other-repos).

**New package only:** turn on pub.dev automated publishing for it first. See [One-time setup](#one-time-setup).
A new package must first exist on pub.dev, so publish its first version by hand with `dart pub publish`.

### What the workflow does

1. It checks that the tag (without `v`) is the root version, and that every package has this version.
   If not, it stops. Run `bin/update_versions.sh` and try again.
2. It gets the publish order from `bin/publish_order.py`.
   Each package comes after the sibling packages it depends on (`dependencies` and `dev_dependencies`).
   Packages with `publish_to: none` are left out. New packages are picked up by themselves.
3. It publishes each package in this order.
   After each one, it waits until `dart pub get` can find the new version.

To see the order on your machine:

```bash
python3 bin/publish_order.py
```

A package is skipped when its version is already on pub.dev.
So if a run fails halfway, fix the problem and click "Re-run jobs". It continues where it stopped.

### Dry run

Open Actions > Release > "Run workflow".
It runs `dart pub publish --dry-run` for every package and publishes nothing.
Warnings (for example a missing CHANGELOG entry) show as yellow warnings. They do not fail the run.

### One-time setup

Do this once for each published package, and for every new package before its first tag.
The list of packages is the output of `python3 bin/publish_order.py`.

On pub.dev:

1. Open `https://pub.dev/packages/<name>/admin`.
2. Under "Automated publishing", click "Enable publishing from GitHub Actions".
3. Repository: `dartondox/dox`.
4. Tag pattern: `v{{version}}`.
5. Tick "Require GitHub Actions environment" and set the environment to `pub.dev`.
6. Save.

On GitHub, in `dartondox/dox` > Settings > Environments, there must be an environment named `pub.dev`.
The publish job runs in it.
Optional: add yourself as a required reviewer, and allow only tags `v*`.

## Packages in other repos

| Package | Repo |
| --- | --- |
| `dox` (the CLI) | [dartondox/dox-cli](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-cli) |
| `dox_orm`, `dox_migration` | [dartondox/dox-orm](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-orm) |
| `dox_auth` | [dartondox/dox-auth](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-auth) |
| `dox_openapi` | [dartondox/dox-openapi](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-openapi) |
| `dox_validation` | [dartondox/dox-validation](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-validation) |
| `dox_socketio` | [dartondox/dox-socketio](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-socketio) |
| `dox_storage` | [dartondox/dox-storage](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-storage) |
| `dox_queue` | [dartondox/dox-queue](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-queue) |
| `dox_scheduler` | [dartondox/dox-scheduler](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-scheduler) |
| `dox_inertia` | [dartondox/dox-inertia](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-inertia) |
| `dox_view` | [dartondox/dox-view](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-view) |
| `dox_mailer` | [dartondox/dox-mailer](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-mailer) |

The packages here use them from pub.dev. The database tests (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite) run in `dox-orm`.
`dox_core` uses `dox_openapi` and `dox_validation`.
CI in this repo uses their newest code: `ci/clone-siblings.sh`, then `ci/use-siblings.sh`.

To work on one of them and Dox together:

1. Clone the repos next to the Dox repo, like `../dox-orm`.
   `ci/clone-siblings.sh` clones `dox-orm`, `dox-auth`, `dox-openapi`, `dox-validation`, `dox-socketio`, `dox-storage`, `dox-queue`, `dox-scheduler` and `dox-cli`.
   Clone `dox-mailer`, `dox-view` and `dox-inertia` by hand when you need them.
2. Add them to the root `pubspec_overrides.yaml` of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file.
   For `dox_openapi` and `dox_validation`, `ci/use-siblings.sh` writes this file for you.

    ```yaml
    dependency_overrides:
      dox_openapi:
        path: ../dox-openapi
      dox_validation:
        path: ../dox-validation
    ```

3. Run `dart pub get`.

The apps in `examples/` already use these clones (their `pubspec_overrides.yaml`), so clone them before you run an example.
In the other repo, a `pubspec_overrides.yaml` that points to `../dox/packages/...` uses your local Dox packages.

Each repo has its own version. Push a `v<version>` tag in that repo to release it.

## Native packages

The three native packages live in their own repos:

| Package | Repo |
| --- | --- |
| `dox_http_native` | [dartondox/dox-http-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-http-native) |
| `dox_postgres_native` | [dartondox/dox-postgres-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-postgres-native) |
| `dox_mysql_native` | [dartondox/dox-mysql-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-mysql-native) |

Dox uses them from pub.dev. Their build hooks download ready-built libraries, so you do not need Rust to work on Dox.

To work on a native package and Dox together:

1. Clone the package next to the Dox repo, like `../dox-http-native`.
2. Add it to the root `pubspec_overrides.yaml` of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file.

    ```yaml
    dependency_overrides:
      dox_http_native:
        path: ../dox-http-native
    ```

3. Run `dart pub get`.

Each native package is released from its own repo, with its own version.
Push a `v<version>` tag in that repo.
Its CI builds the libraries, uploads them, fills the hashes and publishes the package to pub.dev.
Then raise the version constraint in the Dox packages that use it.

## Docs

The docs site is https://dartondox.dev. It is built with MkDocs Material and
[mike](https://github.com/jimporter/mike). mike keeps one folder per version on the `gh-pages` branch.

| URL | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `/3.x/...` | 3.x docs, built from `main` |
| `/latest/...` | a copy of the newest version (now 3.x) |
| `/` | redirects to `/latest/` |
| old links like `/the-basic/routing/` | redirect to `/latest/the-basic/routing/` |

### Write and preview

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve           # live preview of this branch
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict  # the same build as CI. Broken links fail.
```

`hooks/docs_hooks.py` runs during the build. It makes the changelog page from `packages/*/CHANGELOG.md`, and writes `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`.

The `Docs check` workflow (`.github/workflows/docs-check.yaml`) runs on every pull request that changes the docs. It runs three checks:

- `mkdocs build --strict`
- a spell check: `codespell docs --skip "*.svg,*.png,*.ico,*.css,*.js" --ignore-words .codespell-ignore`
- `ci/check-no-tabs.sh`: the docs must not use content tabs

### Deploy

- 3.x deploys with each release. The `Docs` workflow (`.github/workflows/docs.yaml`) runs on a
  `v<version>` tag, the same tag that publishes the packages. So docs for a feature that is not released yet stay off the site.
  It runs `mike deploy --update-aliases 3.x latest`.
- To deploy the docs only (a typo fix, or the docs of a package from another repo that was just released),
  push a `docs-v<version>` tag on `main`, like `git tag docs-v3.0.1-1 && git push origin docs-v3.0.1-1`.
  It publishes no package and runs no tests.
- After each deploy, the workflow writes small redirect pages for the old root links,
  the root `index.html`, a `404.html` and the `CNAME` file. So `dartondox.dev` and old links keep working.
- The workflow pushes with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`. This works because `gh-pages` is not a protected branch.

### New major version

When 4.x starts, deploy 4.x with `mike deploy --update-aliases 4.x latest`. Keep a `v3.x`
branch, and add `3.x` to the workflow input, so 3.x can still be fixed.

# Meet Doxie

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/community/mascot/

# Meet Doxie

![Doxie, the Dox mascot](../assets/mascot.png){ width="260" }

Doxie is the official mascot of Dox. Doxie is a blue dachshund.

## Why a dachshund

"Doxie" is a common nickname for a dachshund. It sounds like Dox, so the name came first.

A dachshund is small, fast and full of energy. Dox tries to be the same: a small native binary that serves a lot of requests.

## Logo and mascot

Dox has a logo and a mascot. They have different jobs.

| | Logo | Mascot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What | A hexagon with a "D" cut out | Doxie, the blue dachshund |
| Where | The docs header, the favicon, the README, pub.dev | The home page, social cards, talks, stickers |
| Files | [`logo.svg`](../assets/logo.svg) (white, for dark backgrounds) | [`mascot.png`](../assets/mascot.png) (transparent background) |

Use the logo when the space is small, like an icon or an avatar. Doxie has too much detail to read well at 16 or 32 pixels.

## Colors

| Name | Hex | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sky blue | `#5CC6FF` | Doxie's body, links in dark mode |
| Dart blue | `#0A5FC2` | Doxie's ears and collar, links in light mode |
| Navy | `#0B1B36` | The docs header, outlines |

## Use Doxie

You are welcome to use Doxie when you write or talk about Dox: blog posts, slides, videos and stickers.
Please do not change Doxie's colors, and do not use Doxie to brand another product.

# Routing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/routing/

# Routing

A route connects a URL and an HTTP method to the code that answers it.

This is the path of one request through the router:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q["Request<br>GET /blogs/42"] --> B["Router<br>method, host, path"]
    B -->|no match| N["404"]
    B -->|match| P["Params as text<br>req.param"]
    P --> M["Middleware"]
    M -->|returns a value| S["Response"]
    M -->|returns the request| T["Typed params, DTO<br>int id"]
    T --> C["Controller"]
    C --> S
```

## Where routes live

Routes are in the `lib/routes` folder. Each file has one `Router` class.
The `prefix` of the router is added in front of all its routes.

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (DoxRequest req) => 'pong'); // GET /api/ping
  }
}
```

Dox finds every `Router` class by itself. It is in `lib/generated/container.g.dart` after `dart run build_runner build`.
To pick the order of routers, list them in `routers:` of `AppConfig`.
See [Dependency injection: routers and providers](dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers).

The leading `/` in a path is optional. `'ping'` and `'/ping'` are the same route.

## Route methods

```dart
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);
Route.put('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.update);
Route.patch('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.update);
Route.delete('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.destroy);
```

!!! info
    There are also `Route.options`, `Route.copy`, `Route.view`, `Route.link`, `Route.unlink`,
    `Route.purge`, `Route.lock`, `Route.unlock` and `Route.propfind`.
    These are HTTP methods. `Route.view` is the WebDAV `VIEW` method. It does not render a template like Laravel `Route::view`.
    To show a template, use a GET route: `Route.get('welcome', (DoxRequest req) => view(req, 'welcome'))` with `view()` of `dox_view`.

    `Route.health('/health')` adds a health check route. It answers `200` with `{"status": "ok"}`.
    `Route.websocket('echo', (WebSocket socket, DoxRequest req) {...})` adds a raw WebSocket route.
    By default any website can open it from a browser, with the cookies of the user. To check the `Origin`, pass `allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com']`, or set `AppConfig(webSocketAllowedOrigins: [...])` for every WebSocket route. Then only pages of the same host and the listed sites can open it. Other origins get `403`. `[]` means the same host only.
    When a WebSocket route has no check, Dox prints one warning to stderr at start.
    A message over `maxMessageSize` bytes (default 16 MB) closes the socket with code `1009`. Example: `Route.websocket('chat', handler, maxMessageSize: 64 * 1024)`.

A `HEAD` request runs the `GET` route of the same path. The answer has the status and headers of `GET`, with no body.

### More than one method

`Route.match` adds the same handler for a list of methods. `Route.any` adds it for `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`.

```dart
Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST'], '/contact', (ContactController c) => c.handle);
Route.any('/webhook', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
```

- `HEAD` comes with `GET`, so do not list it. An unknown method throws an `ArgumentError` at start.
- `Route.any` does not add `OPTIONS`. So Dox still answers the CORS preflight request for the path.
- `.where(...)` and `.timeout(...)` after `Route.match` or `Route.any` work on every route it added. `.name(...)` names the last one.

## Redirect routes

`Route.redirect` sends a path to another URL. The status is `302` by default.

```dart
Route.redirect('/home', '/');
Route.redirect('/old-blog', '/blog', status: 301);
Route.permanentRedirect('/old-pricing', '/pricing'); // 301
```

The redirect works for the same methods as `Route.any`.

- The target is sent as it is. A param like `{id}` in the target is not filled in: `Route.redirect('/u/{id}', '/users/{id}')` sends the client to `/users/{id}`.
- The query string of the request is dropped. `/home?page=2` goes to `/`, not `/?page=2`.
- For these cases, use a normal route and return `redirect(...)` with the URL you build.

## The handler

The second argument is the code that answers the request. It can be:

```dart
// a function
Route.get('/ping', (DoxRequest req) => 'pong');

// a controller method. The controller comes from the container.
Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);

@Inject()
class WebController {
  String pong(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

// a list: middleware first, the controller last
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[
  LoggerMiddleware(),
  (WebController c) => c.pong,
]);
```

In a list, the last item is the controller. The items before it are [middleware](middleware.md).
`(WebController c) => c.pong` picks the method. Dox calls it once per isolate, at start.
See [Dependency injection](dependency-injection.md).

See [Controller](controller.md) for the parameters a handler can ask for.

## Route params

Put a param in `{}`. Ask for it as a typed parameter in the controller.

```dart
Route.get('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<Blog?> show(int id) async {
    return Blog().find(id);
  }
}
```

`/blogs/abc` answers `404`, because `abc` is not an `int`.
See [Controller: parameters](controller.md#parameters) for all the rules.

### Optional param

`{name?}` can be missing. Use a nullable type.

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{page?}', (int? page) {
  return 'page ${page ?? 1}'; // GET /posts and GET /posts/2 both match
});
```

### Catch-all param

`{name*}` matches the rest of the path, with slashes.

```dart
Route.get('/docs/{page*}', (String page) {
  return page; // GET /docs/a/b/c gives 'a/b/c'
});
```

### Param rules

`.where(param, regex)` lets a route match only when the param text matches the regex.
When it does not match, the router tries the next route. When no route matches, the client gets `404`.

```dart
Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).where('id', '[0-9]+');
Route.get('/users/{name}', (UserController c) => c.byName); // gets the rest

Route.get('/files/{type}', handler).where('type', 'png|jpg');
Route.get('/docs/{page}', handler).where('page', '.*'); // matches slashes too
```

- The regex must match the whole param text. You do not need `^` or `$`. A leading `^` and a trailing `$` are dropped.
- Use `(?:...)` for a group, not `(...)`. A regex with a `(...)` group throws an `ArgumentError` at start.
- A param name that the path does not have throws an `ArgumentError` at start.
- Call `.where` more than once for more params.
- Routes without `.where` match the same as before. The check costs nothing for them.
- The regex checks the param text two times: as it is in the URL, and again after `%` codes are decoded. Both checks must pass. A `%` code for a letter, a digit or `-._~` is decoded before the router sees the path, so `/users/%31` is `/users/1` and matches `[0-9]+`. Other `%` codes stay in the URL text and must pass the second check. So `/files/x%2Fy` does not match `[^/]+`, because `%2F` is `/`. The controller gets the decoded value. In the second check, `.` also matches a new line (`%0A`), so `.*` still matches it.

## Group routes

```dart
// by prefix
Route.group('/blogs', () { // (1)!
  Route.get('/', (BlogController c) => c.index); // GET /blogs
  Route.get('/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.show); // (2)!
});

// by domain
Route.domain('dartondox.com', () { // (3)!
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
});

// by middleware
Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () { // (4)!
  Route.get('/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
  Route.post('/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
});
```

1.  `/blogs` goes in front of every path in the callback.
    Dox puts one `/` between the parts. `'blogs'` and `'/blogs/'` work the same.
2.  Makes `GET /blogs/{id}`.
3.  These routes match only when the `Host` header is `dartondox.com`. Other hosts get `404`.
4.  `AuthMiddleware` runs before `me` and `logout`. It runs after the global and router middleware.

Groups can be nested. `Route.group('blogs', ...)` with `Route.get('all', ...)` makes `/blogs/all`.

A group can also add a prefix to the [route names](#named-routes) inside it, with `name:`.

To turn CORS on or off for some routes, see [CORS](../security/cors.md).

## Resource routes

One line makes the usual CRUD routes for a controller.

```dart
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);
```

`BlogController` is a class from the container. A controller object works too: `Route.resource('blogs', BlogController())`.

| Method | Path | Controller method | Route name |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/blogs` | `index` | `blogs.index` |
| `GET` | `/blogs/create` | `create` | `blogs.create` |
| `POST` | `/blogs` | `store` | `blogs.store` |
| `GET` | `/blogs/{id}` | `show` | `blogs.show` |
| `GET` | `/blogs/{id}/edit` | `edit` | `blogs.edit` |
| `PUT`, `PATCH` | `/blogs/{id}` | `update` | `blogs.update` |
| `DELETE` | `/blogs/{id}` | `destroy` | `blogs.destroy` |

The name comes from the path: `/` becomes `.`, and `{params}` are left out.
So `Route.resource('users/{user}/posts', ...)` gives `users.posts.index`.
Pass `name:` to pick another one: `Route.resource('blogs', BlogController, name: 'posts')`.

A method that the controller does not have is skipped. No route is made for it.
Any other error from the controller is not hidden. It stops the app at start, so you see it.
See [Resource controller](controller.md#resource-controller) to make one with the CLI.

## Forms with PUT, PATCH and DELETE

An HTML form can only send GET or POST. To reach a `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` route, add `MethodOverride` to the global middleware.

```dart
AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[const MethodOverride()],
);
```

Then send the form as POST with a `_method` field.

```html
<form method="POST" action="/blogs/5">
  <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="DELETE">
</form>
```

- Only a POST request changes, and only to `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`. Other values are ignored.
- `req.method` gives the new method.
- `CsrfMiddleware` still checks the request, so send the `_token` field too.
- It works only in `globalMiddleware`, not on a router or a route. It is off by default.

A client that can not send PUT, like an old proxy or JS client, can send the `X-HTTP-Method-Override` header instead. Turn it on with `header: true`. It is off by default.

```dart
AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[const MethodOverride(header: true)],
);
```

The header has the same rules as `_method`. When both are there, the header wins.

## Named routes

Give a route a name with `.name()`. Then build its URL from the name, so a path lives in one place.

```dart
Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).name('users.show');

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5});
// /users/5

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5}, query: <String, Object>{'tab': 'posts'});
// /users/5?tab=posts
```

`route()` gives the path. `Route.url()` does the same.
Param values are URL encoded. A missing `{name?}` param is left out.

A group can put a prefix in front of the names inside it:

```dart
Route.group('admin', () {
  Route.get('users', (UserController c) => c.index).name('users'); // admin.users
}, name: 'admin.');
```

Dox stops with a clear error when:

- two routes have the same name (at start),
- `route()` gets a name that no route has,
- a `{param}` of the path has no value, or `params` has a key the path does not have.

### Signed routes

A signed URL is a named route with a `signature` in its query, so nobody can change it. Use it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe".
Protect the route with `ValidateSignature`, and make the URL with `Route.signedUrl`:

```dart
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');

Route.signedUrl('unsubscribe',
    params: <String, Object>{'user': 5}, expires: Duration(days: 7));
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?expires=...&signature=...
```

A changed or expired URL gets `403`. See [Signed URLs](../security/signed-urls.md).

## Route model binding

A binder turns a route param into a value before the controller runs, for example a model from the database.
Add it with `Route.bind`, before the routes that use it.

```dart
Route.bind<User>('user', (String id) => User().find(id));

Route.get('/users/{user}', (DoxRequest req, User user) {
  return user;
});
```

Every route with a `{user}` param now runs the binder first.
The binder gets the raw text from the URL. It returns the value, or `null` when there is none.
`null` answers `404`, the same way as a thrown `NotFoundHttpException`.

There are two ways to read the value:

- Ask for a parameter of the bound type, like `User user`. Dox matches it by type, so it can be at any place in the parameter list.
- Read it from the request: `req.bound<User>('user')`. This also works in a controller that only takes `DoxRequest`.

Other path params still work next to it:

```dart
Route.get('/users/{user}/posts/{page}', (User user, int page) {
  return user.posts(page);
});
```

The binder runs after the middleware, so an auth middleware can stop the request before any database call.

A `@DoxModel` class does not need `Route.bind`. Dox makes a binder for it in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
See [Dependency injection: route model binding](dependency-injection.md#route-model-binding).
`Route.bind` wins when both exist.

## Serve static files

`Route.staticFiles(prefix, folder)` serves the files of a folder, like CSS, JavaScript and images.

```dart
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');
Route.staticFiles('build', 'public/build', maxAge: Duration(days: 365));
```

- Only `GET` and `HEAD` requests read files, and only when no route matches. A route always wins.
- `..`, dot files (like `.env` or `.git`) and folders are never sent. They get `404`.
- The one dot folder that is sent is `.well-known` at the top of the folder (`public/.well-known/...`). It holds ACME (Let's Encrypt) challenges, `security.txt` and `apple-app-site-association`. Dot files inside it still get `404`.
- A file gets a weak `ETag` (from its size and change time) and `Last-Modified`. The browser gets `304` with no body when it already has the file. `If-None-Match` wins over `If-Modified-Since`. Range requests work. With `If-Range`, the Range is used only when it is the file's `Last-Modified` date. Else the whole file is sent.
- `maxAge` sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=...`. Give a long `maxAge` to build files with a hash in the name (like Vite's).
- No middleware runs for a file. The global CORS config still applies.
- Like other routes, the prefix follows `Route.group`, the router prefix and `Route.domain`.
- The folder path is relative to the folder the app starts in. Symlinks in the folder are followed.

!!! warning
    Never save user uploads in this folder. An uploaded html or svg file would run its script on your site.
    Use [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) for uploads. It sends such files as downloads.

Behind a proxy, the proxy can serve the folder instead. Then the files never reach Dox.

## Fallback route

`Route.fallback` answers a `GET` or `HEAD` request that matches no route and no static file.
Use it for a custom 404 page, or to send `index.html` of a single page app.

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/', (WebController c) => c.home);

    Route.fallback((DoxRequest req) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Page not found'}).statusCode(404);
    });
  }
}
```

- Other methods still get the normal `404` or `405`.
- A `GET` to a path that only has a `POST` route gets the fallback, if a fallback covers that path. If none does, the client gets `405`.
- Add the fallback before `startServer()`, like other routes. A fallback added later only works in the isolate that added it. The other isolates do not get it.
- The fallback runs its middleware like any route. Add it in a `Router`, so the global middleware (like security headers) runs too.
- It follows `Route.group`, the router prefix and `Route.domain`. In a group, it only answers paths under the group prefix. A prefix can have params, like `{tenant}`, and `req.param` gives them. When two fallbacks match, the one with the longest prefix wins.
- The handler decides the status. Return a `404` status for a "not found" page, else the client gets `200`.

!!! note
    The built-in `404` and `405` answers do not run the global middleware.
    Running it there could change answers for apps today. For example, `CsrfMiddleware` would answer `419` to a `POST` to an unknown path, and `SessionMiddleware` would start a session for every bad link.
    Use `Route.fallback` in a router when your `404` page needs the global middleware.

## Serve storage files

`Storage.route(path)` from the [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) package serves the files of a storage disk at `GET <path>/{key*}`.
By default only signed URLs work. Other requests get `403`.
See [File Storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md#serve-local-signed-urls).

```dart
Storage.route('files');
Storage.route('public', disk: 'local', signed: false);
```

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is sent as a download (`Content-Disposition: attachment`) with `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox`.
So a script in an uploaded file does not run on your site.
Every file response also has `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so the browser does not guess another type.

For user uploads, `download: true` sends every file as a download, also images and PDFs:

```dart
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);
```

## Request body for the docs

`post`, `put` and `patch` take a `body:` schema. It shows in the [OpenAPI docs](../packages/openapi.md).
It does **not** check the request. To check input, use a [DTO](validation.md).

```dart
Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store, body: v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'title': v.string().min(3),
}));
```

## Mount a raw handler

`Route.mount(prefix, handler)` sends every request under a path prefix straight to a raw `HttpRequest` handler.
It runs before routing and before the body is read. The handler writes and closes the response itself.
[Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md) uses it for `/socket.io/`.

```dart
Route.mount('/socket.io/', io.handle);
Route.mount('/admin', admin.handle, middleware: true);
```

How the prefix matches:

- It matches whole path parts. `/admin` matches `/admin`, `/admin/` and `/admin/users`. It never matches `/administrator` or `/admin-login`.
- A trailing `/` does not change the match. `/socket.io/` also matches `/socket.io`.
- The query string is not part of the match.
- When two prefixes match, the longest one wins. `//` counts as one `/`, so `/admin//secure/x` goes to a mount at `/admin/secure`.
- The match uses the raw path. `%2F` stays encoded, so `/admin/secure%2Fx` goes to a mount at `/admin`. To protect a nested path, set `middleware: true` on the outer mount too.

!!! warning
    By default a mount skips all middleware, also the global middleware (security headers, CSRF, rate limit).
    Set `middleware: true` to run `AppConfig.globalMiddleware` before the handler.
    The global CORS config never applies to a mount. The handler must send its own CORS headers.

With `middleware: true`:

- A middleware that gives a response (like `403`) stops the request. The handler does not run.
- The body is not read for the middleware, so the handler can still read it. A CSRF token must come in a header.
- The handler sends the answer itself. So the part of a `next` middleware that runs after the handler cannot change the answer.
- A `terminate` step runs once the answer is sent, like on other routes.
- `RequestTimeout` does not run for a mount. The handler already owns the answer.
- Cookies that a middleware adds after the handler (the session cookie, `XSRF-TOKEN`) are not sent. Get the CSRF token from a normal route.
- An error in the handler gives `500`, like without middleware.

# Request

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/request/

# Request

This page shows how to read input, files, headers and cookies from a request.

## Typed input (recommended)

Ask for a [DTO](validation.md) in your controller. Dox reads the body (or the query for `GET`, `HEAD` and `DELETE`), checks it, and gives you a typed object.

```dart
Route.put('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User?> update( // (1)!
    int id, // (2)!
    UpdateUser input, // (3)!
  ) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    user?.name = input.name;
    await user?.save();
    return user;
  }
}
```

1.  The return value is the response. Dox waits for a `Future`.
    A `String` is sent as text. A `Map` or a model is sent as JSON.
2.  A path param. It is `{id}` from the route. `/users/abc` answers `404`, because `abc` is not an `int`.
3.  A DTO. Dox reads the body, checks it, and builds the object before this method runs.

Bad input gets `422` before your method runs. See [Validation](validation.md).

## Raw input

Add a `DoxRequest` parameter to read the raw values. These values are **not** checked.

```dart
@Inject()
class ApiController {
  String sayHello(DoxRequest req) {
    String? name = req.input('name');
    return 'Hello $name';
  }
}
```

| Code | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `req.input('name')` | one value from the query string or the body. The body wins when both have the key. |
| `req.input('user.name', 'guest')` | a value inside a map or list, with a dot key. The second value is the default, used when the key is not there or is null. |
| `req.all()` | all values from the query string and the body, as a `Map` |
| `req.only(<String>['name', 'email'])` | only these keys |
| `req.except(<String>['password'])` | all values, without these keys |
| `req.has('name')` | `true` when the key is there as it is and not empty. It does not read dot keys. |
| `req.filled('name')` | `true` when the key is there and not empty. A text of only spaces, an empty list and an empty map count as empty. |
| `req.exists('name')` | `true` when the key is there, with any value (also `''` or null) |
| `req.missing('name')` | `true` when the key is not there |
| `req.boolean('remember')` | `true` for `true`, `1`, `on` and `yes`. Else `false`. |
| `req.integer('page', 1)` | the value as an `int`. The default is used when the key is not there or is not a number. |
| `req.body` | the body only (JSON, form data) |
| `req.query` | the query string only |
| `req.add('key', value)`, `req.merge({...})` | add values, for example in a middleware |

A dot key reads inside the input. `req.input('items.0.id')` gives the `id` of the first item.
A key that is in the input as it is wins. So a body key `'a.b'` is read before the `b` key inside `a`.
Dot keys also work in `filled`, `exists`, `missing`, `boolean`, `integer`, `file` and `hasFile`.
`has` does not read dot keys: `req.has('user.name')` is `false` for `{"user": {"name": "Ann"}}`. Use `filled` for that.

Form and query keys with brackets give lists and maps, like in Laravel:

| Input | `req.input(...)` gives |
| --- | --- |
| `tags[]=a&tags[]=b` | `req.input('tags')` is `['a', 'b']` |
| `address[city]=Yangon` | `req.input('address')` is `{'city': 'Yangon'}` |
| `items[0][name]=x` | `req.input('items')` is `[{'name': 'x'}]` |
| `name=a&name=b` (no brackets) | `req.input('name')` is `'b'`, the last value |

## Route params

Ask for a path param as a typed parameter, like `int id` in the example above.
The text values are also in `req.param`, like `req.param['id']`.
They are URL-decoded: `/users/a%20b` gives `'a b'`.
See [Controller: parameters](controller.md#parameters).

## Form data (File)

An uploaded file is a `RequestFile`. The request must be `multipart/form-data`.
Put the file in a DTO, so Dox checks its type and size:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart"
@Inject()
class ApiController {
  Future<Map<String, String>> uploadImage(UploadImage input) async {
    String uploadedPath = await input.image.store('images');
    return <String, String>{'filename': uploadedPath};
  }
}
```

`store()` comes from the [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) package. Add it and import `package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart`.

Without a DTO, `req.file('image')` gives the `RequestFile`, or null when the field is not a file.
`req.hasFile('image')` is `true` when the field holds a file or a list of files.
For a field with many files, use `req.input('images')`. The file is not checked.

### `RequestFile`

```dart
RequestFile file = req.input('video');

file.filename;        // name from the client
file.filetype;        // content type, like video/mp4
file.extension;       // mp4
file.length;          // size in bytes
await file.size;      // size in KB
file.stream();        // read it in chunks
await file.store('videos');              // save to storage (needs dox_storage). returns the path
await file.moveTo('/data/videos/1.mp4'); // move it. returns the new File
await file.bytes;     // the whole file in memory. avoid for big files
```

!!! warning "Save the file before you return"
    A file up to 1 MB stays in memory. A bigger file is written to a temp file while it arrives.
    The temp file is **deleted when the response is sent**.
    So call `store`, `moveTo` or `stream` before your controller returns.

### Size limits

A body that is too big gets `413 Payload Too Large`. Dox checks `Content-Length` first.
It also counts the bytes while it reads the body.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig(
  maxBodySize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,        // JSON and urlencoded, default 10 MB
  maxMultipartSize: 100 * 1024 * 1024,  // form-data uploads, default 100 MB
);
```

Set the same limit in your proxy, like `client_max_body_size` in nginx.

## Headers

```dart
String? token = req.header('X-Token');
Map<String, dynamic> all = req.headers; // a repeated header is joined with ', '

req.userAgent();  // User-Agent header
req.host();       // Host header
req.origin();     // Origin header, or null
req.referer();    // Referer header, or null
req.isJson();     // true for a JSON body
req.isFormData(); // true for multipart/form-data
req.locale;       // first language of Accept-Language, like 'th', or null
req.bearerToken(); // the token of 'Authorization: Bearer <token>', or null
```

## Path and URL

```dart
req.path();                   // '/admin/users/5'
req.fullUrl();                // 'https://example.com/admin/users/5?tab=info'
req.pathIs('admin/*');        // true. `*` matches any text
req.routeIs('admin.users.*'); // true when the route name matches
```

`pathIs` cleans the path like the router does. A `/` at the start or the end does not matter, and `//` counts as one `/`. So `'admin/*'` and `'/admin/*'` are the same, and `/admin/` and `/admin//` match `'admin'`, like they reach the `/admin` route.
`routeIs` is `false` for a route with no name. Give a route a name with `.name('admin.users.show')`.

## Cookies

```dart
String? token = req.cookie('token');                 // decrypted value
String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);   // value as sent
```

See [Response](response.md#cookie) to set a cookie.

## Client IP and scheme

```dart
req.ip();       // client IP
req.scheme();   // http or https
req.isSecure(); // true for https
```

Behind a proxy, `req.ip()` shows the proxy, not the client.
Set `trustedProxies` in `AppConfig` to fix it. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md#https-put-a-proxy-in-front).

# Response

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/response/

# Response

This page shows what a controller can return, and how to set the status, headers and cookies.

## Return a value

Return the value from your controller. Dox turns it into the response.

| You return | The client gets |
| --- | --- |
| a `String` | the text |
| a `Map` or a `List` | JSON |
| a model, a list of models, a [serializer](serializer.md) | JSON (from `toJson()`) |
| a `DateTime` | the ISO 8601 text |
| an `IHttpException`, like `NotFoundHttpException()` | its status code and JSON: `{"code": ..., "message": ...}`, or a `Map` message as it is |
| a `File` (from `dart:io`) | the file, streamed |
| a `Stream<List<int>>` | the bytes, streamed |
| `StreamFile`, `DownloadableFile` (also from `Storage()` of `dox_storage`) | the file, streamed |
| `response(...)` | full control: status, headers, cookies |

```dart
// JSON
Map<String, String> hello(DoxRequest req) {
  return <String, String>{'message': 'hello world!'};
}

// a model
Future<Blog?> show(int id) async {
  return Blog().find(id);
}
```

## Errors

Throw or return an exception to answer with an error.

| Exception | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `BadRequestException()` | `400` |
| `NotFoundHttpException()` | `404` |
| `PayloadTooLargeException()` | `413` |
| `UnsupportedMediaTypeException()` | `415` |
| `TokenMismatchException()` | `419` |
| `ValidationException()` | `422` |
| `TooManyRequestsException()` | `429` |
| `InternalErrorException()` | `500` |

Each one takes `message:`, `errorCode:` and `code:`:

```dart
throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'Blog not found');
```

The client gets `404` with `{"code":"not_found","message":"Blog not found"}`.
`code` is the `errorCode`. A `Map` message is sent as it is.

For another status, extend `IHttpException`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ForbiddenException extends IHttpException {
  ForbiddenException({String message = 'Forbidden'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.forbidden;
    super.errorCode = 'forbidden';
    super.message = message;
  }
}
```

Any other error gets `500`. It is also passed to the [exception handler](errors.md).

## Files and big responses

Return a `File` or a `Stream<List<int>>`. Dox sends it in chunks. It does not load it all into memory.

- A `File` sets `Content-Type` (from the file name), `Content-Length` and `Accept-Ranges`.
- It answers `Range: bytes=...` with `206 Partial Content`. Video players can seek, and downloads can resume.
- `Storage().stream()` and `Storage().download()` on the local disk also stream the file.

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

// a file from disk
Route.get('/video', (DoxRequest req) => File('storage/video.mp4'));

// a download from Storage
Future<DownloadableFile> download(DoxRequest req) async {
  // sends Content-Disposition, so the browser saves the file
  return Storage().download('report.pdf');
}

// a stream from Storage
Future<StreamFile> show(DoxRequest req) async {
  return Storage().stream('photo.jpg');
}
```

See [File Storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md).

## The `response()` helper

Use `response(content)` when you need to set the status, headers or cookies.
All methods return the response, so you can chain them.

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

DoxResponse store(DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'status': 'created'})
      .statusCode(201)
      .header('X-Request-Id', 'abc')
      .contentType(ContentType.json);
}
```

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `statusCode(201)` | sets the status code. Default `200`. |
| `header('X-Key', 'value')` | sets one header |
| `withHeaders({...})` | adds these headers. A key replaces the header with the same name, in any case. Other headers stay. |
| `contentType(ContentType.html)` | sets `Content-Type` (`ContentType` is from `dart:io`) |
| `cache(Duration(minutes: 5))` | sets `Cache-Control: max-age=300` |
| `cookie(DoxCookie(...))` | sets a cookie |
| `content(value)` | changes the body |
| `stream(byteStream)` | sends a `Stream<List<int>>` as the body |

## Redirect

```dart
// 302 to a path
return redirect('/login');

// another status
return redirect('/posts', status: 301);

// back to the page the request came from (Referer), or '/'
return back(req);
```

See [Session](session.md#redirect-back-with-errors) for flash messages and errors with a redirect.

## Cookie

```dart
// set a cookie
DoxCookie cookie = DoxCookie('theme', 'dark');
return response('ok').cookie(cookie);

// set a cookie with options
DoxCookie token = DoxCookie(
  'token',
  'value',
  maxAge: Duration(days: 7), // sent as Max-Age in seconds. default 1 hour
  httpOnly: true, // default true: page scripts can not read it
  secure: true,   // default: Secure only when the request came over https
  path: '/',
  sameSite: SameSite.lax, // from dart:io. default: none sent
);
return response('ok').cookie(token);

// delete a cookie
return response('ok').cookie(DoxCookie('token', ''), setExpire: true);
```

To read a cookie, see [Request: cookies](request.md#cookies).

!!! info "Encrypt and decrypt"
    By default, Dox encrypts the cookie value with `APP_KEY`, and decrypts it when you read it.
    To turn this off, use `DoxCookie(key, value, encrypt: false)` to set it,
    and `req.cookie(key, decrypt: false)` to read it.

## Change every response

To change every response in one place (for example, to add a header), set a `responseHandler` in `AppConfig`.

```dart title="lib/app/http/handler.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    return res.header('X-Powered-By', 'Dox');
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  // ...
);
```

# Views

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/views/

# Views

Views are HTML templates.

Dox fills them with your data and sends them as the response.

The `dox_view` package has a template engine like Edge.js. Templates are `.dox.html` files in `resources/views`.

## Install

```bash
dart pub add dox_view
```

Add the provider in `lib/`, so every isolate sets up the engine:

```dart title="lib/providers/view_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart';

class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());
}
```

## Render a view

`view()` renders a template and sends it as HTML. Leave out the `.dox.html` extension.

```dart
DoxResponse show(DoxRequest req) {
  return view(req, 'users/show', <String, dynamic>{
    'user': user,
    'posts': posts,
  });
}
```

This renders `resources/views/users/show.dox.html`:

```html
<h1>{{ user.name }}</h1>
```

`View.render()` gives the HTML as a string, for example for an email:

```dart
String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
```

## Output

`{{ }}` prints a value. It escapes HTML, so a user can not add a `<script>` tag to your page.

```html
<p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
```

`{{{ }}}` prints a value with no escape. Use it only for HTML you trust.

```html
<article>{{{ post.html }}}</article>
```

`null`, and a variable that does not exist, print nothing.

A comment is not in the output:

```html
{{-- only you see this --}}
```

To print `{{` or a tag as text, put `@` before it: `@{{ name }}` prints `{{ name }}`, and `@@if` prints `@if`.

### Stay safe

`{{ }}` escapes HTML. It does not make every place in a page safe.

- **Always quote attributes.** Write `href="{{ url }}"`, not `href={{ url }}`.
  Without quotes, a space in the value starts a new attribute, like `onclick=...`.
- **Check URLs from users.** `href="{{ url }}"` does not block a `javascript:` URL.
  A click on `javascript:alert(1)` runs the code.
  Allow only `http://` and `https://` URLs (or your own paths) before you print them.
- **`<script>` and `<style>` are not safe.** Inside them, `{{ }}` only escapes HTML.
  It does not make a value safe for JavaScript or CSS.
  Do not print user data there. Put it in a quoted `data-` attribute, and read it in your script.

```html
<a href="{{ profile.website }}">Website</a>  {{-- only after you check it is http or https --}}

<div id="app" data-user-name="{{ user.name }}"></div>
<script>
  const name = document.getElementById('app').dataset.userName;
</script>
```

## Expressions

Inside `{{ }}` and tags, you can use:

| What | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Values | `'text'`, `"text"`, `42`, `1.5`, `true`, `false`, `null` |
| Lists and maps | `[1, 2]`, `{ name: 'Ann', 'full name': 'Ann Lee' }` |
| Fields | `user.name`, `user?.name`, `items[0]`, `map['key']` |
| Math | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `~/` |
| Compare | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` (`===` and `!==` work too) |
| Logic | `&&`, `\|\|`, `!`, `a ?? b`, `a ? b : c` |
| Functions | `route('users.show', { id: 5 })`, `name.toUpperCase()` |

`+` joins text: `{{ 'Hi ' + name }}`.

Fields work on maps, and on objects with a `toJson()` method, like Dox models.

Lists, maps and text have `length`, `isEmpty` and `isNotEmpty`. Lists also have `first`, `last`, `contains()`, `join()` and `indexOf()`.
Text has `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `trim()`, `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `endsWith()`, `split()`, `replaceAll()`, `substring()` and `indexOf()`.
Numbers have `toStringAsFixed()`, `round()`, `floor()`, `ceil()` and `abs()`.

In `@if` and `?:`, these values are false: `null`, `false`, `0`, `''`, an empty list and an empty map.

## Conditions

```html
@if(user.isAdmin)
  <a href="/admin">Admin</a>
@elseif(user.isEditor)
  <a href="/posts">Posts</a>
@else
  <p>Welcome</p>
@end
```

`@unless(x)` is `@if(!x)`.

A tag alone on its line leaves no empty line in the output.

A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit, so `me@mail.com` stays text. Put a space before the tag, or use `{{ on ? 'active' : '' }}`.

## Loops

```html
<ul>
  @each(user in users)
    <li>{{ user.name }}</li>
  @else
    <li>No users yet</li>
  @end
</ul>
```

The `@else` part shows when the list is empty.

Get the index too, or the key of a map:

```html
@each((user, index) in users)
  {{ index + 1 }}. {{ user.name }}
@end

@each((value, key) in settings)
  {{ key }}: {{ value }}
@end
```

`$loop` has `index`, `first`, `last` and `length`:

```html
@each(tag in tags)
  {{ tag }}{{ $loop.last ? '' : ', ' }}
@end
```

## Variables

`@let` makes a variable. `@assign` changes it.

```html
@let(total = 0)
@each(item in cart)
  @assign(total = total + item.price)
@end
Total: {{ total }}
```

## Partials

`@include` puts another template in this one. It sees the same variables.

```html
@include('partials/nav')
@includeIf(user, 'partials/account')
```

## More tags

Close a block tag with `@end`. `@else` works in all of them, but not in `@once` and `@verbatim`.

Put `@auth`, `@guest`, `@production`, `@once` and `@verbatim` alone on their line. In the middle of text, like `@once upon a time`, they stay text.

| Tag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@isset(user.phone) ... @end` | shows when the value is not `null`. A field of `null` is not an error here. |
| `@empty(items) ... @end` | shows when the value is false: `null`, `false`, `0`, `''`, an empty list or map |
| `@auth ... @end` | shows when the user is logged in (`req.auth`) |
| `@guest ... @end` | shows when the user is not logged in |
| `@env('local') ... @end` | shows when `APP_ENV` is this value. A list works too: `@env(['local', 'staging'])`. Case does not matter. |
| `@production ... @end` | shows when `APP_ENV` is `production` |
| `@once ... @end` | shows only the first time in one render, for example a `<script>` in a component |
| `@verbatim ... @end` | prints the text as it is: no `{{ }}` and no tags run inside it |

```html
@auth
  <a href="/logout">Log out</a>
@else
  <a href="/login">Log in</a>
@end
```

`@auth` and `@guest` use the `req.auth` that `view()` gets. In `View.render` there is no request, so `@guest` shows.

`@verbatim` ends at the first `@end`, so the text inside can not have `@end`. Use it for code of a JavaScript framework that also uses `{{ }}`:

```html
@verbatim
  <div id="app">{{ message }}</div>
@end
```

These tags print an HTML attribute:

```html
<a @class(['link', { active: isActive, muted: !isActive }])>Home</a>
<input type="checkbox" name="news" @checked(user.news)>
<option value="en" @selected(lang == 'en')>English</option>
<button @disabled(saving)>Save</button>
```

- `@class` takes text, a map of class name to a condition, or a list of these. It prints `class="..."` with the names whose condition is true. The names are escaped.
- `@checked`, `@selected` and `@disabled` print the attribute name when the value is true.

A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit. Write `on @else off`, not `on@else off`.

When `resources/views/components/` has a template with the same name, like `class.dox.html`, the component wins.

## Layouts and components

A component is a template with its own props and slots. Use one for the page layout.

```html title="resources/views/layouts/main.dox.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>{{ title ?? 'My app' }}</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>{{ $slots.header }}</header>
    <main>{{ $slots.main }}</main>
  </body>
</html>
```

```html title="resources/views/home.dox.html"
@component('layouts/main', { title: 'Home' })
  @slot('header')
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
  @end

  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
```

- The second argument is the props. In the component they are variables (`title`), and also `$props.title`.
- `@slot('name') ... @end` fills a named slot. Everything else goes into `$slots.main`.
- A slot is HTML, so `{{ }}` does not escape it again.
- `$slot` is the same as `$slots.main`. Both are always there. They are empty when the component has no body.
- A component only sees its props, `$props`, `$slots`, `$slot`, `$attributes`, the globals and the request helpers of `view()` (see [Forms](#forms)). It does not see the variables of the page.

`@!component(...)` is a component with no body and no `@end`.

### Components as tags

A template in `resources/views/components/` is also a tag with its name. A `.` in the tag is a folder.

```html title="resources/views/components/button.dox.html"
<button class="btn btn-{{ type ?? 'primary' }}">{{ $slots.main }}</button>
```

```html
@button({ type: 'danger' })
  Delete
@end

@!form.input({ name: 'email' })   {{-- components/form/input.dox.html --}}
```

### Attributes

`$attributes` has the props as HTML attributes. `{{ $attributes }}` prints them, like `id="save" title="Save"`. The values are escaped.

`$attributes.merge({ ... })` adds default attributes. A prop wins over a default, but `class` is joined:

```html
<button {{ $attributes.merge({ class: 'btn', type: 'button' }) }}>{{ $slot }}</button>
```

```html
@button({ class: 'btn-big', type: 'submit' })
  Save
@end
```

This prints `<button class="btn btn-big" type="submit">`.

Only text, numbers and `true` are attributes. `true` prints the name alone, like `hidden`. `null`, `false`, lists, maps and objects are left out. You can still read any prop, like `$attributes.type`.

`$attributes` keeps any attribute name, like `onclick`. So do not pass a map from the user as the props of a component.

## Forms

With `SessionMiddleware`, `view()` adds these to every template:

| Name | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `csrfField()` | the hidden `_token` field for `CsrfMiddleware` |
| `csrfToken()` | the CSRF token |
| `errors` | the flashed validation errors, like `errors.email` |
| `old('email')` | the input of the request before |
| `session('key')` | a value from the session |

If your app has a global named `errors`, the global shows when the request has no validation errors. When there are validation errors, they win over the global.

```html
<form method="POST" action="/register">
  {{ csrfField() }}
  <input name="email" value="{{ old('email') }}">
  @if(errors.email)
    <p class="error">{{ errors.email }}</p>
  @end
  <button>Register</button>
</form>
```

Every template from `view()` also has `request.path`, `request.method` and `request.query`.

Components and layouts see all of these too, so a layout can use `request.path` and a form component can use `csrfField()`.

## Globals

Globals are variables and functions that every template can use. `route()` is there by default.

```dart
const ViewConfig(globals: <String, Object?>{'appName': 'My app'});

View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
View.global('money', (num cents) => (cents / 100).toStringAsFixed(2));
```

```html
<footer>{{ appName }} {{ year }}</footer>
<a href="{{ route('users.show', { id: user.id }) }}">Profile</a>
<p>{{ money(order.total) }}</p>
```

You can add globals before or after `View.configure()`. The engine keeps them. When a name is in both, the value in `ViewConfig.globals` wins.

Each isolate has its own engine. So add globals in your provider, after `super.setup()`. Then every isolate gets them:

```dart title="lib/providers/view_provider.dart"
class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
  }
}
```

A value of type `SafeString` is printed with no escape:

```dart
View.global('logo', const SafeString('<img src="/logo.svg" alt="Logo">'));
```

## Config

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | `resources/views` | the folder of the templates |
| `extension` | `.dox.html` | the file extension |
| `cache` | on, but off when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local` | keep parsed templates in memory |
| `globals` | `{}` | variables for every template |

With the cache off, a changed template shows on the next request, with no restart.

## Errors

A syntax error, or an error in an expression, throws a `ViewException`. The message has the template name and the line:

```
ViewException: expected ")" but found the end (in "users/show", line 12)
```

## Prettier

Prettier formats `.html` files, and it does not know the `@` tags. Add this line to `.prettierignore`:

```
*.dox.html
```
