# File Storage

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/file-storage/

# File Storage

`Storage()` saves and reads files on a disk: the local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory.

It is in the [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) package. A new project already has it.

```dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putRequestFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});
```

## Config

A new project already has `lib/config/storage.dart`, with one `local` disk in the `storage` folder.
`STORAGE_DISK` in `.env` picks the default disk.
To add disks, edit the file. This example adds a `url` to the local disk, an `s3` disk and a `memory` disk:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for signedUrl(); url() gives /storage/<path> without it
    },

    /// only when AWS_BUCKET is set
    if (env.awsBucket != null)
      's3': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 's3',
        'bucket': env.awsBucket,
        'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
        'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
        'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
        'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
      },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);
```

A local disk writes a file in place by default. To write to a temp file and rename it when the write is done, add `'atomic_writes': true` to the disk. A failed or stopped upload then never leaves a partial file, and the old file stays. It is off by default.
The rename makes a new file. So the folder must be writable, the file gets the default mode and the owner of the app, a hard link keeps the old content, and a symlink is replaced.

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'atomic_writes': true},
```

The `s3` disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to
`lib/config/env.dart` and run `dart run build_runner build`. They are nullable,
and the `s3` disk is only added when `AWS_BUCKET` is set. So the app starts without them:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;
```

The provider of a new project sets these disks in every isolate. It is in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

| Driver | Options |
| --- | --- |
| `local` | `root` (default `storage`), `url`, `app_key` (default: your APP_KEY), `visibility` |
| `s3` | `bucket`, `region`, `key`, `secret`, `token`, `endpoint`, `path_style` (MinIO), `url` (CDN), `visibility`, `acl`, `batch_delete` |
| `memory` | none. For tests |

The `s3` disk needs `bucket`, `key` and `secret`. When one is missing, the app stops at start with an `ArgumentError` that names the setting.

## Functions

```dart
// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path2 = await Storage().putRequestFile('images', file);
String path3 = await Storage().putRequestFileAs('avatars', 'user-1.png', file); // your own name

Uint8List? bytes = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing
bool found = await Storage().exists(path);            // files only
bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');
await Storage().delete(path);

int size = await Storage().size(path);                 // throws when missing
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path); // throws when missing

await Storage().append('logs/app.log', 'new line');    // a missing file is made
await Storage().prepend('logs/app.log', 'first line');
await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');              // local disk only

String url = await Storage().url(path);         // /storage/<path> when the disk has no `url`
String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path); // the same as signedUrl()

// another disk
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports', bytes, extension: 'pdf');
```

On a local disk with no `url` option, `url()` gives `/storage/<path>` (no host). Dox serves it only when you add `Storage.route('storage', signed: false)`. `signedUrl()` still needs `url`.

`get()` gives `null` for a missing file, but `size()` and `lastModified()` throw `FileNotFoundException`.

`append()` and `prepend()` add a new line between the old and the new text, but only when the file is not empty. Change it with `separator`.
They keep the visibility and content type of the file.
They read the file and write it back, so two writers at the same time can lose a write.

`makeDirectory()` makes a folder only on a local disk. On any other disk it does nothing.

`exists()` finds files only. `directoryExists()` finds folders. On a local disk it checks the real folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is under it.

`putRequestFile` on the local disk moves the upload temp file. It does not read it into memory.

An uploaded file can store itself. `store` gives it a new uuid name. `storeAs` uses your name, and replaces an old file with the same name. Both take `disk:`:

```dart
RequestFile file = req.input('image');
String path = await file.store('images');
String onS3 = await file.store('images', disk: 's3');
String avatar = await file.storeAs('avatars', 'user-1.png');
```

`storeAs` and `putRequestFileAs` use the name as it is. Do not use the file name from the client. Make your own name, like `user-1.png`.

`putRequestFile` and `file.store()` take the extension from the file name. When the bytes are a known format (png, jpg, pdf, zip, ...) that does not match the name, the extension of the bytes is used. So a png sent as `a.html` is saved as `.png` and is never served as a web page.

### `stream` and `download`

```dart
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});
```

Both read the file as a stream, from any disk, with `Content-Length`.
A big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers `404`.

### Full disk API

`Storage().use('s3')` returns the `dox_storage` `Disk`: `copy`, `move`, `listAll`, `getMetaData`,
`putStream`, `setVisibility` and more. See [dox_storage](../packages/storage.md).

## Serve local signed URLs

```dart
// lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk than the default
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download
```

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site.
Every file has `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

```dart
String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...
```

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers `403`.
Signed URLs work only on a `local` disk. For another disk, use `signed: false`.
A signed URL works only on the route of its own disk.
An old signed URL, made before the disk name was part of the signature, still works on any local disk with the same app key. This ends when it expires.
Set the disk `url` option to the full URL of the route (`https://app.test/files`).

## Tests

To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see [Testing](testing.md#test-file-storage).

## Your own driver

Implement `DriverContract` from `package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart`. Register it in a [provider](providers.md), so every isolate has it:

```dart
Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes', bytes, extension: 'txt');
```

# Environment Variables

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/env/

# Environment Variables

Declare your env keys once, in a typed class.

Then `env.appPort` is an `int`, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup.

## The typed env class

A new project already has `lib/config/env.dart`. Its keys are listed in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-a-new-project). This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after each change to the class. It writes `env.g.dart`. Then use `env` anywhere:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
```

### The rules

- **Key**: the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. `appName` reads `APP_NAME`, `s3Bucket` reads `S3_BUCKET`. Use `@EnvKey('X')` for another name.
- **Default**: the getter body. It can be any expression, like `Platform.numberOfProcessors`. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can not read another env getter.
- **Optional**: a nullable getter with no body (`String? get s3Bucket;`). It is `null` when the key is missing.
- **Required**: any other getter with no body. A missing key stops the app.
- **Empty**: an empty value (or the text `null`) counts as missing.

### Types

| Type | Value in `.env` |
|------|-----------------|
| `String` | any text |
| `int`, `double`, `num` | `3000`, `0.5` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off` (any case) |
| `Uri` | `https://dox.dev` |
| `Duration` | a number and a unit: `500ms`, `30s`, `5m`, `2h`, `1d`. A plain number is seconds: `300` is 5 minutes. |
| an enum | the name of a value, any case: `debug` |
| `List<String>` | comma separated: `a, b, c`. Empty items are dropped. |

Any other type is a build error.

### Fail fast

`AppEnv.load()` reads every key one time. Then it checks them all, and throws one `EnvException` that lists every missing or bad key:

```
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int, not "abc"
```

This happens once, when the app starts. After that, `env.dbPort` is a plain field read.

## Where values come from

Dox reads values from these places:

1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
2. In tests only: the `.env.testing` file. See [Testing: a test database](testing.md#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting).
3. The `.env` file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

!!! info "The environment wins"
    A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.
    So you can keep `.env` for development and use real variables in production.

### The `.env` file

```ini title=".env"
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=3f9a1c7e5b2d4f6a8c0e1b3d5f7a9c2e
DB_PORT=5432
```

- One `KEY=value` per line.
- Quotes around a value are removed. So `APP_NAME="My app"` gives `My app`. Use `"`, `'` or `` ` ``.
- A `=` inside the value is kept: `TOKEN=a=b` gives `a=b`.
- A line that starts with `#` is a comment.
- A `#` after a space starts a comment: `APP_PORT=3000 # dev` gives `3000`.
- A `#` with no space before it is kept: `DB_PASSWORD=abc#123` gives `abc#123`.
- A `#` inside quotes is kept: `DB_PASSWORD="abc # 123"` gives `abc # 123`.

## Commands

```bash
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key
```

`dox env:generate` reads `.env.example`:

- digits become an `int` with that default: `APP_PORT=3000` gives `int get appPort => 3000;`
- `true`/`false` become a `bool` with that default
- an empty value becomes an optional `String?`
- any other value becomes a required `String`. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
- `#` comment lines above a key become its doc comment

It does not overwrite an existing `lib/config/env.dart`. Run `dox build_runner:build` after it.

`dox env:check` exits with code 1 when a key is missing or bad. Use it in CI or before a deploy.

## Tests

To pass your own values in a test, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-env).

## Env.get: the low-level way

`Env.get()` reads one key by name. Use it for a key you only know at run time. For normal config, use the typed class.

```dart
Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set
```

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

- `String` gives an empty string `''`. It is never the text `"null"`.
- `String?` and `dynamic` give `null`. With no type, like `Env.get('KEY')`, the type is `dynamic`, so you get `null`.
- `int`, `num`, `double` and `bool` throw an `ArgumentError` with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

`Env.get()` looks up and converts the value on every call. Do not call it on a hot path.

!!! warning "APP_KEY"
    When `APP_KEY` is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, `Dox().startServer()` stops with an error.
    When `APP_ENV` is `development`, `local`, `test` or `testing`, it only logs a warning. Make a key with `dox key:generate`.

# Isolate

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/isolate/

# Isolate

This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

## How it works

Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own [native server](native-server.md) on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

- Linux: each isolate has its own socket (`SO_REUSEPORT`).
- macOS: the isolates share one socket.
- Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

Each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]
```

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See [How Dox works](../concepts/how-dox-works.md#where-the-database-pools-live).

## How many isolates

By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (`Platform.numberOfProcessors`).

To change it, set `totalIsolate` in `lib/config/app.dart`. A new app reads it from `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);
```

You can also set it in code, before `startServer()`. This wins over the config:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();
```

Use fewer isolates when:

- the machine also runs the database or other heavy work, or
- you use Socket.IO rooms without the Redis adapter. A room only reaches clients on the same isolate. Use `1`, or see [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md).

## Each isolate has its own memory

Isolates do not share memory:

- A static value or a singleton exists once **per isolate**. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
- The `memory` cache store is per isolate. See [Cache](cache.md).
- To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

`Dox().isolateId` tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is `1`.

## What each isolate does at start

Dox copies the `AppConfig`, the providers and the routes you added before `startServer()` to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

1. runs `setup()` of each provider (for example, it opens the database pool),
2. registers the routes of your routers,
3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
4. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in `setup()`. See [Providers](providers.md).

## When an isolate crashes

- An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a `500` and keeps going.
- An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The isolate keeps running.
- If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints `[dox] isolate N exited, restarting` to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
- If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker `restart:` or systemd `Restart=always`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#keep-it-running).

# Providers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/providers/

# Providers

A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app when it starts, for example the database, auth or a Redis connection.

A provider has two methods:

- `setup()` runs when the app starts. You must write it.
- `shutdown()` runs when the app stops. It is optional.

## Why providers

Dox runs your app on many [isolates](isolate.md), and they do not share memory.
Code that you run once in `bin/server.dart` only sets up the first isolate. The others have, for example, no database connection.
A provider fixes this: each isolate runs `setup()` itself.

## Create a provider

Extend `DoxProvider` and put your code in `setup()`. `setup()` can be `async`. Dox waits for it.

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

## Register it

You do not need to. Dox finds every class that extends `DoxProvider`.
Run `dart run build_runner build`. The provider is then in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.
Each isolate makes its own instance from the container. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container.
See [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers).

Providers run in the order of their file path. To run one first, list it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);
```

A listed provider runs first. Then the others run. No provider runs twice.

You can also add a provider in code, before `startServer()`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Example: auth

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}
```

The name is `AppAuthProvider`, because `dox_auth` already has a class named `AuthProvider` (it finds the user model).
See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md).

## When `setup()` runs

In each isolate, Dox runs `setup()` of each provider, one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container.
Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a provider set up.
See [What each isolate does at start](isolate.md#what-each-isolate-does-at-start).

`dox openapi:generate` also runs `setup()` of every provider, because it needs the routes.

## Clean up on shutdown

On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` Dox stops the server gracefully (see [Deployment](deployment.md#graceful-shutdown)).
After the open requests are done, it runs `shutdown()` of every provider.
It runs in every isolate. Use it to close connections or flush data.
A provider that has nothing to close does not need to write `shutdown()`.

The `ORMProvider` of a new project already does this: its `shutdown()` calls `SqlQueryBuilder.close()`.
Dox closes the cache stores (eg. Redis) by itself, after the providers.

```dart title="lib/providers/redis_provider.dart"
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}
```

An error in `shutdown()` goes to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The other providers still run.

## Rules for a provider

- **Open connections in `setup()`, not in the constructor.** A provider listed in `AppConfig` is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
- **Keep `setup()` short.** It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.

# Dox CLI

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/dox-cli/

# Dox CLI

The `dox` CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Every `make:*` command also answers to its `create:*` name.
Run `dox help` to see all commands. Run `dox help <command>` for one command.

## Installation

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
```

!!! warning "Add the pub bin folder to your PATH"
    If your shell can not find `dox`, add this line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, and open a new terminal:

    ```bash
    export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
    ```

To remove the CLI:

```bash
dart pub global deactivate dox
```

## All commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dox create <name> [--version <v>]` | create a new project |
| `dox serve` (or `dox s`) | start the dev server with build_runner watch |
| `dox build` | build the native (AOT) bundle into `build/bundle` |
| `dox build_runner:watch` / `dox build_runner:build` | run the code generator |
| `dox make:controller <name> [-r]` | create a controller |
| `dox make:middleware <name>` | create a middleware |
| `dox make:dto <name>` | create a DTO (typed, checked input) |
| `dox make:serializer <name>` | create a serializer |
| `dox make:model <name> [-m]` | create a model, and with `-m` its migration |
| `dox make:migration <name> [--sql]` | create a Dart migration, or a `.sql` one with `--sql` |
| `dox migration:run` (or `dox migrate`) | run new migrations |
| `dox migration:rollback [--step=N]` | undo the last batch, or the last N migrations |
| `dox migration:reset` | undo all migrations |
| `dox migration:refresh` | undo all, then run all again |
| `dox migration:fresh` (or `migrate:fresh`) | drop all tables, then run all migrations |
| `dox migration:status` | show which migrations ran, and their batch |
| `dox make:factory <model>` | create a model factory in `db/factories`, see [Factories](../database/factories.md) |
| `dox make:seeder <name>` | create a seeder in `db/seeders` (and `bin/seed.dart`), see [Seeders](../database/seeders.md) |
| `dox db:seed [--class=<name>]` | run `DatabaseSeeder`, or another seeder |
| `dox make:job <name>` | create a queue job in `lib/app/jobs` (and `bin/queue.dart`) |
| `dox queue:work [--queue=a,b] [--concurrency=N] [--once] [--tries=N] [--timeout=S] [--sleep=S] [--stop-when-empty] [--timeout-grace=S]` | run the queue worker |
| `dox queue:failed` | list the failed jobs |
| `dox queue:retry <id\|all>` | put a failed job (or all) back on the queue |
| `dox queue:forget <id>` | delete one failed job |
| `dox queue:flush` | delete all failed jobs |
| `dox queue:clear [queue]` | delete the jobs of a queue |
| `dox queue:restart` | stop the running workers after their current jobs |
| `dox queue:prune-failed [--hours=N]` | delete failed jobs older than N hours (default 24) |
| `dox queue:table` | create a migration for the `jobs` and `failed_jobs` tables (from the `dox_queue` package) |
| `dox auth:tokens-table` | create a migration for the `auth_access_tokens` table (from the `dox_auth` package) |
| `dox schedule:work` | run the scheduler and keep it running |
| `dox schedule:run` | run the tasks that are due now, once |
| `dox schedule:list` | list the scheduled tasks |
| `dox schedule:test <name>` | run one scheduled task now |
| `dox key:generate [--show] [--force]` | make a new `APP_KEY`. `--show` prints a key and writes nothing. In production it asks first, `--force` skips |
| `dox env:generate` | make `lib/config/env.dart` (the typed env class) from `.env.example`, see [Environment Variables](env.md) |
| `dox env:check` | check the env against `lib/config/env.dart`. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) |
| `dox openapi:generate [dir]` | run `bin/openapi.dart` to write `openapi.json` and `openapi.yaml` (default `storage/openapi`). A new project has no `bin/openapi.dart` yet, see [OpenAPI](../packages/openapi.md#write-the-files-dox-openapigenerate) |
| `dox update` | update the CLI |
| `dox version` (or `dox -v`) | show the CLI version |
| `dox help [command]` | show help |

## Project

### Create a project

```bash
dox create new_blog
dox create new_blog --version <release tag>
```

`dox create` copies the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template from GitHub. Without `--version`, it uses the newest template release with the same major version as the CLI.

- The folder name is the project name in snake case: `NewBlog` makes `new_blog`.
- It makes `.env` from `.env.example`, with a new `APP_KEY`.
- Then run `cd new_blog`, `dart pub get` and `dox serve`.

### Run the dev server

```bash
dox serve                         # or: dox s
dox s --ignore-build-runner       # do not run build_runner watch
```

`dox serve` runs `dart run bin/server.dart` and restarts it when a `.dart` file changes.
It also runs `build_runner watch`, so generated files stay up to date.

### Build for production

```bash
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).

## Create files

```bash
dox make:controller Blog        # lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
dox make:controller Blog -r     # resource controller
dox make:middleware Auth        # lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart
dox make:dto CreateBlog         # lib/app/dtos/create_blog/create_blog.dto.dart
dox make:serializer Blog        # lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart
dox make:model Blog -m          # lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart and a create_blogs_table migration
dox make:migration create_blogs_table          # .dart file (default)
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql    # .sql file
```

- `-r` adds the methods `index`, `create`, `store`, `show`, `edit`, `update` and `destroy`.
- Word breaks are kept. `BlogPost` makes `blog_post.controller.dart` with the class `BlogPostController`.
- After `make:controller` or `make:dto`, run `dox build_runner:build` (or keep `dox serve` running). See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md).
- The table of a model is its name in plural snake case: `BlogPost` makes `blog_posts`. The model gets `@DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts')`.

## Migrations

### Database settings

The migration commands read the database settings from the `.env` file and the real environment. A real environment variable wins.

```ini title=".env"
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
```

- `DB_CONNECTION` defaults to `postgres`. The default port is `5432` for postgres and `3306` for mysql.
- `DB_DATABASE` works too, in place of `DB_NAME`.
- `DATABASE_URL` wins over all the `DB_*` keys when it is set.
- Put comments on their own line. A `#` after a value becomes part of the value.

All keys are in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-the-framework).

### Run and undo migrations

```bash
dox migration:run                # or: dox migrate
dox migration:status
dox migration:rollback           # undo the last batch
dox migration:rollback --step=2  # undo the last 2 migrations
dox migration:reset              # undo all migrations
dox migration:refresh            # undo all migrations, then run them again
dox migration:fresh              # drop all tables, then run all migrations
```

`migrate:rollback`, `migrate:reset`, `migrate:refresh`, `migrate:fresh` and `migrate:status` also work.
Add `--seed` to `migration:run`, `migration:refresh` or `migration:fresh` to run the seeders after it.

- A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1.
- On MySQL, statements like `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

## Update the CLI

`dox update` installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI.
To pick the version yourself, run the install command again.

# Package commands

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/package-commands/

# Package commands

A package can add its own `dox` commands.

Your app can add its own commands too.
You do not write a `bin` file, and you do not register anything.
The `dox` CLI finds the commands by itself.

For example, `dox queue:table` comes from the `dox_queue` package, and `dox auth:tokens-table` comes from the `dox_auth` package.

## Use a package command

Add the package and run `dart pub get`. Then run the command:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue
dox queue:table
```

`dox help` lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

## Add a command to your package

### 1. Write the command

A command extends `Command` from `package:dox_core/command.dart`.

```dart title="lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}
```

`dox hello:say Ann` calls `run(['Ann'])`. The words after the name are the `args`.

### 2. List the commands

Make one library with a top-level `commands` list:

```dart title="lib/commands.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];
```

### 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart
```

The value must be a library of the package itself, like `package:my_package/commands.dart`. Use only letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` and `/` in the path, and no `..`. That is all. An app that depends on your package now has `dox hello:say`.

## Add a command to your app

It works the same way. Put the command in `lib/` of your app, and add the key to the app's own `pubspec.yaml`:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dox:
  commands: package:my_app/commands.dart
```

## Exit codes and errors

- When `run` ends, `dox` exits with code 0.
- To fail, set `exitCode` from `dart:io` (like `exitCode = 1`), or throw. A thrown error is printed with its stack trace, and the exit code is 1.
- The exit code of the command is the exit code of `dox`, so scripts and CI see it.

## Write a migration

A command can add a migration file with `MigrationFile`. The file gets the same name as `dox make:migration` makes, like `2026_10_21_120000_create_queue_tables.dart`.

```dart
String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}
```

`create` returns `null` and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there, with any time in its name. `dox migrate` writes `db/migration/migrations.dart` again before it runs, and makes `bin/migrate.dart` when it is missing. So `dox migrate` runs the new file.

## Rules

- A built-in command always wins. When a package has a command with the same name as a built-in one, `dox` runs the built-in one. `dox help` marks the package command as not used.
- When two packages have a command with the same name, `dox <name>` prints an error with both package names, and exits with code 1.
- A bad `dox: commands:` key (not a library of the package, or a file that is not there) prints a warning with the package name. The commands of the other packages still work.
- An unknown command prints `Could not find a command named "<name>"`, with a hint about the `dox: commands:` key.

## How it works

1. `dox <name>` first looks for a built-in command.
2. Then it reads `.dart_tool/package_config.json`, and the `dox: commands:` key in the `pubspec.yaml` of each package and of the app.
3. It writes `.dart_tool/dox/commands.dart`. This file imports each commands library and runs the command with your args.
4. It runs that file with `dart run`.

`dox` writes the file again only when `.dart_tool/package_config.json`, your `pubspec.yaml`, or the `pubspec.yaml` of a package change. So after `dart pub get`, or after you change the key in a local package. When a package had a warning (like a commands library that is not there yet), `dox` looks again on the next run. The code of the commands is always the newest, because `dart run` compiles it each time.

`dox help` keeps the list of package commands in `.dart_tool/dox/commands.json`. It loads the list again when a package or a commands library (the file in the key) changes. When you change only a file that the commands library imports, `dox help` can show the old description until then. The command itself always runs the new code.

An app inside a pub workspace works too, also when the `workspace:` list uses a glob like `apps/*`. `dox` finds the workspace root from `.dart_tool/pub/workspace_ref.json`, which `dart pub get` writes in each member.

# Deployment

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/deployment/

# Deployment

This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

!!! danger "Never run production with `dart run`"
    `dart run` (and `dox serve`) uses the JIT compiler. It is made for
    development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB
    instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for
    production.

## Build

```bash
dox build
```

This makes a `build/bundle/` folder:

| File                        | What it is                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `build/bundle/bin/server`   | the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it  |
| `build/bundle/bin/queue`    | the queue worker, when `bin/queue.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/bin/schedule` | the scheduler, when `bin/schedule.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/lib/`         | native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite)   |
| `build/bundle/db/`          | your `db/` folder (migrations, seeders). SQLite database files are left out |
| `build/bundle/.env.example` | copy it to `build/bundle/.env`, or use env variables |

`dox build` runs `build_runner` (when your app uses it), then
`dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build`. It builds
`bin/queue.dart` and `bin/schedule.dart` the same way, when they exist.
It exits with code 1 when a step fails, so CI can stop.

!!! warning "Not `dart compile exe`"
    `dox_orm` depends on `sqlite3` v3. It bundles SQLite with a build hook.
    `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error.
    `dart build cli` is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks.
    Keep `bin/` and `lib/` together: the binary loads the libraries from `../lib`.

Start it:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

The binary reads `.env` and `db/` from the folder you start it in.
A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in `bin/server.dart`, before the server starts.
So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

## Docker

A new Dox app has this multi-stage `Dockerfile`. The final image is `FROM scratch`: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle, `db/`, `libgcc_s` and an empty `/tmp`.

```dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get
COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline
RUN dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
RUN dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build

# the queue worker and the scheduler are binaries too
RUN dart build cli --target bin/queue.dart --output build/queue \
  && cp build/queue/bundle/bin/queue build/bundle/bin/ \
  && dart build cli --target bin/schedule.dart --output build/schedule \
  && cp build/schedule/bundle/bin/schedule build/bundle/bin/

RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r db /out/app/db \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

The image has no `.env` file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as
environment variables:

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env -e DB_HOST=... my-app
```

A new app also has a `docker-compose.yml`. It runs the app, a queue worker and Postgres, and reads `.env` with `env_file: .env`:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

A new `.env` uses SQLite. The compose services set `DB_CONNECTION=postgres` and `DB_NAME=dox` themselves. To use the compose Postgres with `dox s`, set the same two values in `.env`. The database port listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes. The compose file has a `worker` service for the queue. In the image, start them with `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
See [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image.

## HTTPS: put a proxy in front

Dox serves plain HTTP only. Its [native server](native-server.md) has no TLS.

Run Dox on plain HTTP on a private port. Put [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com)
or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

By default Dox listens on all network interfaces. When the proxy runs on the
same machine, set `APP_HOST=127.0.0.1`. Then the app port can not be reached
from outside.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx<br>TLS, HTTP/2, gzip, body size limit"]
    X -->|"plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:3000"| D["Dox binary<br>bin/server, one isolate per core"]
    D -->|"one shared pool"| DB[("Database")]
    M["Migrations<br>bin/server.dart runs them once, before the server starts"] --> DB
```

Then tell Dox to trust the proxy, so `req.ip()` and `req.scheme()` show the
real client:

```dart
AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
```

- `req.ip()` reads `X-Forwarded-For`. Dox walks the list from the right and
  skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
- `req.scheme()` reads `X-Forwarded-Proto` (`http` or `https`).
  `req.isSecure()` is true for `https`.
- `trustedProxies` is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers,
  because any client can send them.
- `['*']` trusts any direct client. Only use it when the app port is not
  reachable from outside. With `*`, `req.ip()` is the right-most
  `X-Forwarded-For` hop, the one your proxy added. If you have two proxies
  in a row, list their IPs or ranges instead.

### Caddy

Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets `X-Forwarded-For` and
`X-Forwarded-Proto`. Websockets work with no extra config.

```
example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

### Nginx

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
```

### Pass the real `Host` header

Behind a proxy, the proxy must pass the real `Host` header to Dox, like `proxy_set_header Host $host;` above.
Some checks compare the request with this header:

- the WebSocket origin check (`allowedOrigins` on `Route.websocket`, or `AppConfig.webSocketAllowedOrigins`): a page of the same host can open a socket.
- `back()`: it only goes back to a page of the same host.
- `allowedOrigins` of socket.io.

If the proxy sends its own host (like `localhost:3000`) instead, pages of your site look like another site.
Then sockets from your own pages get `403`, and `back()` goes to the fallback.

## Behind a load balancer

A load balancer keeps idle connections to Dox open, and sends new requests on them.
Dox closes a connection with no request for 30 seconds.
If the balancer keeps it longer, it may send a request on a connection Dox just closed.
Then the client gets `502`.

To fix this, set `idleTimeout` longer than the balancer's idle timeout.
AWS ALB keeps idle connections for 60 seconds, so use 65 seconds:

```dart
AppConfig(
  // ...
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 65),
)
```

## Keep it running

When a worker isolate dies, Dox starts it again. When the main isolate dies,
the process exits with a non-zero code (see [Isolate](isolate.md#when-an-isolate-crashes)).
Let a supervisor restart it: `restart: unless-stopped` in Docker compose,
or `Restart=always` in systemd.

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## Graceful shutdown

On `SIGTERM` (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly, systemd) or `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), Dox stops gracefully, in every isolate:

1. It stops taking new connections at once.
2. Open requests can finish. Each keep-alive connection closes after its current answer.
3. After `shutdownTimeout` (default 8 seconds), it closes the connections that are still open.
4. It runs `shutdown()` of every provider (see [Providers](providers.md#clean-up-on-shutdown)). The `ORMProvider` of a new project closes the database connections here.
5. It closes the cache stores of `Cache()`, eg. the Redis connections.
6. The process exits with code `0`.

A second `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` stops the process at once.

Set the timeout in `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart
AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  ...
)
```

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

| Platform | Waits | Change it with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docker stop` | 10 seconds | `docker stop -t 30`, or `stop_grace_period` in compose |
| Kubernetes | 30 seconds | `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` |
| Cloud Run | 10 seconds | can not be changed |
| Fly.io | 5 seconds | `kill_timeout` in `fly.toml` |
| systemd | 90 seconds | `TimeoutStopSec` |

In code, `await Dox().stop()` does steps 1 to 5 and does not exit.

## Many processes or machines

One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to
run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime.
Run each one on its own port (or machine) and list them in the proxy:

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}
```

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each
process has its own memory.


---

# Native server

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/native-server/

# Native server

Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package `dox_http_native`.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with
WebSocket or Socket.IO routes.

- Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP. It runs on the isolate's own
  thread, so a request never waits for another thread.
- All your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware, ORM.
- It is much faster than the `dart:io` server: about 5 times more requests
  on one or two cores. See [Performance](performance.md).

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your
system when you build the app.

## Without Dox

`dox_http_native` also works on its own, in any Dart app:

```bash
dart pub add dox_http_native
```

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}
```

- `NativeHttpServer.bind(port, address: '127.0.0.1')` listens on one host.
  With no address, it listens on all interfaces.
- `NativeHttpServer.bind(port, maxConnections: 10000)` stops accepting new
  connections at the limit, until one closes. Default: no limit.
- `close()` waits for open requests. `close(force: true)` closes every
  connection at once.

The rest of this page is the same with or without Dox.

## How it works

The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses
   the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.
3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

Under load there is no other thread, so a request never waits for a thread
to wake up. When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread
watches the sockets. When a request comes, it wakes the isolate once. Then
the isolate takes over again.

The loop gives the event loop a turn after a few batches, so timers,
database answers and other async work of the isolate still run on time.
A slow synchronous handler holds the sockets of its isolate, like in Node
and Bun. `await` is fine.

The native server has the same API as the `dart:io` `HttpServer`. So
`req.httpRequest`, `HttpResponse` and code written for `dart:io` keep working.

Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See [Isolate](isolate.md).
The OS spreads connections, not requests. A keep-alive connection stays on
one isolate. So a few busy connections (eg. from one proxy or a load test
with few connections) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections
than isolates.

## When the library does not load

Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to
fix it:

```
Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...
```

`<reason>` is for example `native library ABI 8, expected 9`: the library on
disk is from another version of the package. See
[Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.md#the-native-http-library-did-not-load).

## WebSocket

Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol.

1. Rust marks a request that asks for an upgrade.
2. Dart runs the route, the middleware and the `Origin` check, like for any
   request. A normal answer (eg. `403`) refuses the upgrade.
3. When Dart accepts, Rust sends the `101` answer. From then on Rust
   answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and
   checks the size of each message.
4. Dart gets whole messages, in the same batches as requests. It sends
   messages back the same way as answers.

- A message or frame over the size limit closes the socket with code `1009`.
  Dart never reads it. `NativeWebSocket.upgrade` takes `maxMessageSize`. Socket.IO uses
  `maxHttpBufferSize`.
- Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed. A small compressed
  message could grow very big in memory.
- On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code `1001`.
- In your own code, use `NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request)` from
  `dox_http_native`. It gives a `dart:io` `WebSocket`.

## Threads

Each isolate does its own socket work on its own thread. Each server also
has two small helper threads: one watches the sockets while the isolate is
idle, one does gzip (only with `compress: true`). Under load both sleep.

## Limits

- Max size of the request line plus headers: 16 KB. Bigger gets `431`.
- A bad request gets `400`.
- A multipart form over `maxMultipartSize`, or any other body over
  `maxBodySize`, gets `413` from Rust. When `Content-Length` is too big and
  the client sent `Expect: 100-continue`, the `413` comes before the body is
  sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the
  `413`. Dart checks the limits again.
- A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds (idle time) gets `408`.
  A slow but steady upload is fine.
- A request head must arrive within 30 seconds. A keep-alive connection
  with no request for 30 seconds is closed.
- A client that does not read its answer for 30 seconds is cut off.
- A request with both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
  gets `400`. A transfer encoding other than `chunked` gets `501`.
- At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer, and at most
  1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that
  connection until the answers go out.
- A streamed response with a `contentLength` must send exactly that many
  bytes. `add()` throws when the body passes it, and `close()` fails when
  it is shorter.
- A small response is sent in one piece when it is closed. A streamed
  response (a file, a download, any `Stream`) over 64 KB goes out in
  parts: the client gets the first bytes early. At most 1 MB of it waits
  in memory. Dart reads more of the file only when the client has read
  what was sent. When the client leaves, Dart stops reading.
- A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
- `compress: true` in `AppConfig` works: Rust gzips the body on a helper
  thread, so the isolate does not wait. A streamed response is not compressed.
- WebSocket: one turn reads at most 256 KB of one socket, so one busy
  client can not hold the isolate. While more than 256 KB waits to be sent
  to a client (eg. pongs for a client that does not read), the server stops
  reading its frames.

## Security notes

- Run it behind a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx) on the internet. The proxy
  does HTTPS, buffers slow clients and caps connections.
- Set `maxConnections` when the app port is open to the internet.
- Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port (macOS
  shared socket, Linux `SO_REUSEPORT`). Do not run untrusted code as the
  user of the app.
- `req.uri` resolves `..` in the path. Never build a file path from the
  raw path. Use the storage helpers.

## Where the library comes from

The build hook of `dox_http_native` (`hook/build.dart`) picks the first one
that works:

1. A path you give in the root `pubspec.yaml` of your app:

    ```yaml
    hooks:
      user_defines:
        dox_http_native:
          lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so
    ```

2. A local build in `native/target/release` of the package (for work on
   the package itself).
3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256.
   There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and
   Windows (x64).
4. A build from source with `cargo`, when Rust is installed.

This order is for the package from pub.dev. For a git or path dependency,
step 4 comes before step 3, because the source can be newer than the release.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the
error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

!!! note "Use `dart build cli`"
    `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks. Use `dox build` or
    `dart build cli`. See [Deployment](deployment.md).

## Work on the native code

`dox_http_native` lives in its own repo:
[dartondox/dox-http-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-http-native).
The Rust code is in its `native` folder.

```bash
cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1
```

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see
[Contribute](../community/contribute.md#native-packages).

# Performance

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/performance/

# Performance

This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

The short version:

1. Build with `dox build` and run the AOT binary. Never `dart run` in production.
2. Put Caddy or nginx in front for HTTPS and gzip.
3. Keep the default isolates (one per CPU core).
4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

## Benchmark

The rules of [the-benchmarker/web-frameworks](https://github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks):
each server answers `GET /` (empty body), `GET /user/:id` (the id) and
`POST /user` (empty body). Dox is a full Dox app with these three routes.
"Dox server only" is `dox_http_native` with no framework, to show what the
framework costs.

This only measures the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on
the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. See
[App benchmark](#app-benchmark).

### Why it is fast

The server runs on the isolate's own thread. One FFI call writes the
answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Dart runs the
handlers and calls again. A request never waits for another thread to
wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate
has nothing to do. See [Native server](native-server.md#how-it-works).

A profile with `perf` (4 server cores, 64 connections) shows the effect:

| | Dox | Bun |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU time per request | 4.85 µs | 5.5 µs |
| Context switches per request | 0.08 | 0.035 |

### How it was run

- Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), `linux/arm64`.
- One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on
  different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host
  network, keep-alive.
- wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds
  per route.
- Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
- Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
- Dart 3.13.6, AOT build with `dart build cli` (this is what `dox build`
  does). `dox_core` and `dox_http_native` as released when these numbers were measured. Node 26.12, Bun 1.4.4, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.

How it was run: the same rig as the [benchmark](#how-it-was-run) above.
The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4.
Each server has 4 database connections per core, 8 in total. One run of 15
seconds per route. `dox_postgres_native` and `dox_mysql_native` as released when these numbers were measured.

### Dart VM flags

We tried a bigger young generation (`DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64`
and `128`) for a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise,
and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set. Dox never sets VM
flags for you. `DART_VM_OPTIONS` is read by the AOT binary from
`dox build`, so you can try your own.

## Database drivers

One find-by-id query, AOT build (`dart build cli`), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

| Database | One query at a time | Many queries in flight | App CPU time per query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres 14 (4 connections) | 60 µs | 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) | |
| MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) | 67 µs | 11 µs each (32 in flight) | 13.5 µs |
| MariaDB 11 (10 connections) | 63 µs | 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) | 12.4 µs |

- The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
- Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
- One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

## Bodies, uploads and big responses

These are on by default. You only need to keep them:

- A body over `maxBodySize` or `maxMultipartSize` gets `413` from the native server, before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).
- An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file, so it does not fill the memory. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile).
- A `File` or `Stream` response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses).

## gzip

gzip in Dart is off by default.

```dart
AppConfig(compress: true);
```

- It saves bandwidth, but costs CPU on every response. The native server
  gzips on a Rust thread. Streamed responses are not compressed.
- A proxy (Caddy, nginx) does it better. Turn it on in Dart only when there
  is no proxy.
- Only a body over 256 bytes is gzipped, and only when the client accepts
  gzip. The gzipped body still gets a `Content-Length`.

## Logging

`LogMiddleware` prints one JSON line per request. Writing to stdout blocks
the isolate. So Dox collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every
64 KB) in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of request logs can
be lost. Errors from `Logger` are still written right away.

Turn `LogMiddleware` off when a proxy already writes access logs. The new
project does this for you: `enabled` is `false` when `APP_ENV` is
`production` or not set.

Leave `responseHandler` unset when you do not need it. With no handler, a
plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a `DoxResponse`.

## What Dox does for you

- Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not
  on every request.
- The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on
  every request.
- JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with
  `Content-Length` set.

# Testing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/testing/

# Testing

This page shows how to test a Dox app with the `test` package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

## Setup

A new app from `dox create` already has the `test` package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

```bash
dart pub add dev:test
```

Put your tests in the `test/` folder. Run them with:

```bash
dart test
```

## Test HTTP routes

`DoxTestClient` from `package:dox_core/testing.dart` starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it.

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}
```

- `DoxTestClient.start(appConfig)` runs your providers (like the ORM provider) and adds your routes, the same as a real start.
- It listens on `127.0.0.1` and a free port that the OS picks. So it does not clash with `dox serve`, and many test files can run at the same time.
- It runs on one isolate. `serverPort` and `totalIsolate` of the config are not used.
- `client.close()` stops the server and runs `shutdown()` of every provider (for example, it closes the database).
- With one isolate, you can also add a route inside a test with `Route.get(...)`. It works right away.

### Send requests

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `get(path)` | `GET`. The path can have a query: `'/api/users?page=2'`. |
| `post(path, body: ...)` | `POST`. Also `put`, `patch` and `delete`. |
| `send('OPTIONS', path)` | any other method |
| `headers: {...}` | extra headers for one request |
| `withHeaders({...})` | a copy of the client that sends these headers on every request |
| `withToken(token)` | a copy of the client that sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |
| `withSession()` | a copy of the client that keeps cookies and sends the CSRF token, like a browser. See [Keep a session](#keep-a-session-cookies-and-csrf). |

A `Map` or `List` body is sent as JSON. A `String` or `List<int>` body is sent as it is.
Redirects are not followed, so you can check a `302` and its `Location` header.

### Check the response

| Member | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `res.status` | the status code, like `200` |
| `res.body` | the body as text |
| `res.json` | the body read as JSON |
| `res.header('content-type')` | one header (any case) |
| `res.headers` | all headers, with lower case names |

The `expect` methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

```dart
res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
```

| Method | Fails when |
| --- | --- |
| `expectStatus(200)` | the status is another one. The message shows the body. |
| `expectJson(value or matcher)` | the JSON body does not match. Use a `Map`, or a matcher like `containsPair('id', 1)`. |
| `expectBody(value or matcher)` | the text body does not match |
| `expectHeader(name, value or matcher)` | the header does not match. Use `isNull` for "not there". |

### Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)

`client.withSession()` gives a client that works like a browser:

- It keeps the cookies of every response and sends them back.
- It removes a cookie when the response deletes it (an empty value, `Max-Age=0` or an old `Expires`).
- On `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` it sends the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header, like axios and Inertia. So `CsrfMiddleware` lets the request in.
- It does not follow redirects, so you can check a `302` or `303`.

```dart
test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});
```

- Each `withSession()` call gives a new browser with no cookies.
- `browser.cookies` has the kept cookies (name to raw value). You can read and change them.
- A copy made from it (for example with `withHeaders`) shares its cookies.
- The normal client keeps no cookies. To send cookies once, use `withCookies(res.cookies)`.

### Log in as a user

Make a token, then send it with `withToken`:

```dart
TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);
```

## Test the cache

`Dox().cache` is the `CacheManager` that `Cache()` uses. Replace it with a memory store, so tests do not write files or need Redis:

```dart
setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});
```

A new `CacheManager` in `setUp` gives each test an empty cache. See [Cache](cache.md).

## Test file storage

`Storage.manager.fake(name)` (from `dox_storage`) swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. `restore(name)` puts the real disk back.

```dart
setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .put('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});
```

- Call `Dox().initialize()` first. Without the `StorageProvider` running, `Storage.manager` has only the `local` disk. Start the app, or set the disks yourself: `Storage.manager = StorageDiskFactory().create(storageConfig);`.
- `Storage()` paths start with `/`. A `Disk` key does not, so remove the first `/` when you ask the `Disk` directly.
- A disk also has `assertExists(key)` and `assertMissing(key)`, like `await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf')`. They throw a `StateError` when the check fails.

See [File Storage](file-storage.md).

## Use a test database with `.env.testing`

Put the values for tests in a `.env.testing` file, next to `.env`:

```ini title=".env.testing"
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory
```

When the app runs its tests, Dox reads `.env` first and then `.env.testing`.
A key in `.env.testing` wins over the same key in `.env`. Keys that are only in `.env` stay.

- "Runs its tests" means `dart test`, or a real `APP_ENV=testing` environment variable.
- A real environment variable still wins over both files. So CI can run `DB_NAME=ci_test dart test`.
- It works for `Env.get()` and for the typed `AppEnv.load()`.
- Outside tests, `.env.testing` is never read.

## Test the env

Pass your own values to `AppEnv.load()`. Then nothing is read from the shell or the `.env` file:

```dart
AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);
```

A missing or bad key throws an `EnvException`. So you can also test that your app stops on a bad env. See [Environment Variables](env.md).

## Test the database

A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in `setUpAll`.
Then empty the tables before each test with `refreshDatabase()` from `package:dox_orm/testing.dart`:

```dart title="test/user_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
```

- `refreshDatabase()` empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay. It keeps the rows of the migrations table (`dox_db_migration`).
- It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Foreign keys are not checked while it empties the tables.
- `refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries'])` keeps the rows of more tables.
- Use a separate test database. Set its name in [`.env.testing`](#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting), or in the env of the test run (`DB_NAME=app_test dart test`). Never run it on a database with real data.
- A test without the server can start the ORM with `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig)`.

See [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md) for a full example with SQLite.

!!! tip "Run test files one by one"
    `dart test` runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one: `dart test --concurrency=1`.

# Health check

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/health-check/

# Health check

A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

## Add the route

Add it in `register()` of a router:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
@override
void register() {
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
  Route.health('/health');
}
```

`GET /health` answers `200` with:

```json
{"status": "ok"}
```

## Check the database and the cache

Give named checks. Each check is a function. Put the `Route.health` call in `register()`, as above:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);
```

When all checks pass, the answer is `200`:

```json
{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}
```

When one check fails, the answer is `503 Service Unavailable`:

```json
{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}
```

A check fails when it:

- throws an error,
- returns `false`,
- or takes longer than `timeout` (default 5 seconds).

The checks run at the same time.

- `HealthCheck.cache()` writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. `HealthCheck.cache('redis')` checks the store with that name.
- Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

## Error details

The error of a failed check is passed to `exceptionHandler.report()`, so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in `errors`) only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.
In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

## Change the timeout

```dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);
```

!!! tip
    A route in a router gets the middleware of that router and the global middleware.
    Put `Route.health` in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets `401`.

## See also

- [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image
- [Deployment](deployment.md)


---

# Database

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/

# Database

Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the `dox_orm` package.

- [Query builder](query-builder.md): build SQL with methods.
- [Models](model/index.md): one class per table.
- [Transactions](transactions.md): many queries that succeed or fail together.
- [Migration](migration.md) and [Schema](schema.md): create and change tables.

This is how a query travels from your code to the database:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["Model or QueryBuilder"] --> S["SQL text<br>quoted names, @values"]
    S --> D{"Driver"}
    D --> N["Native Rust pool<br>dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native"]
    D --> T["sqlite3"]
    N --> DB[("Database")]
    T --> DB
```

## Install

The query builder and the models are in the `dox_orm` package.

```bash
dart pub add dox_orm
```

```dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
```

## Supported databases

| Database | `Driver` | Driver | Pool | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postgres | `Driver.postgres` | [`dox_postgres_native`](postgres-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| MySQL 8+ and MariaDB | `Driver.mysql` | [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| SQLite | `Driver.sqlite` | `sqlite3` | No, one connection per isolate | Development, tests, small apps |

!!! info "Native drivers"
    Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. There is no other driver.
    When the native library can not load, the app stops with an error.
    See the [Postgres](postgres-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) and
    [MySQL](mysql-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) pages.

## Config

Put the connections in `lib/config/database.dart`.
`connection` is the name of the default connection.

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 3306,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName, // file path, like db/dox.sqlite, or ':memory:'
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);
```

`env` is the typed env of the app, in `lib/config/env.dart`.
Change `my_app` to the name of your app in `pubspec.yaml`.

- `debug: true` prints each SQL query and its values. The app template turns it on only in development.
- `user`, `password`, `host` and `port` are not used by SQLite.

Start the ORM in a provider. The app template already has this file.
Each isolate runs the provider.
Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process.

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

Dox finds every `DoxProvider` class on its own.
After you add a provider, run `dart run build_runner build`.

### `.env`

The app config and the [migration](migration.md) commands read these values.

```py title=".env"
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like db/dox.sqlite
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres
```

### `DATABASE_URL`

Many hosts (Fly, Render, Heroku and others) give you one database url.
Dox reads it from the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable.

The rule: **when `DATABASE_URL` is set, it wins.**
It replaces the config of the default connection (`DatabaseConfig.connection`).
That config still gives `debug`, `printer` and `extra`.
Other named connections do not change.

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
```

| Form | Database |
|---|---|
| `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` or `postgresql://...` | Postgres |
| `mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db` or `mariadb://...` | MySQL, MariaDB |
| `sqlite:///abs/path.db`, `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:db/dox.sqlite` | SQLite |

- The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write `@` in a password as `%40`.
- No port: `5432` for Postgres, `3306` for MySQL.
- For Postgres, `sslmode` works like libpq (`disable`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`). `require` does not check the certificate. Use `verify-full` when your host supports it. See [Postgres TLS](postgres-native.md#tls).
- For MySQL, `ssl=true` (or `sslmode=require`) turns TLS on, and it checks the certificate. Add `verifyCertificate=false` to skip the check, only for a self-signed certificate in development.
- `host=/path` (or `socket=/path`) connects to a Unix socket, like `host=/cloudsql/project:region:instance`. See [Unix socket](#unix-socket).
- Any other option goes to `extra`, like `?maxConnectionCount=20`. A number becomes an `int`, `true` and `false` a `bool`.

The ORM reads `DATABASE_URL` from the real environment, not from `.env`.
To use a url from `.env`, or any other url, give it yourself:

```dart
DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: {...},
  url: Env.get<String?>('DATABASE_URL'),
);
```

An empty `url` (`url: ''`) turns `DATABASE_URL` off.
To make one `ConnectionConfig` from a url, use `ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url)`.
[Migrations](migration.md#database-settings) read `DATABASE_URL` too, also from `.env`.

### Unix socket

A host that starts with `/` is a Unix socket.
