# ManyToMany

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/many-to-many/

# ManyToMany

Use `ManyToMany` when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side.

For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists.

The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table.
It has one foreign key to each side.

## Tables

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `artist` | `id`, `name` |
| `song` | `id`, `title` |
| `artist_song` (pivot) | `id`, `artist_id`, `song_id` |

A migration for the pivot table:

```dart
await schema.create('artist_song', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('artist_id').constrained('artist').cascadeOnDelete();
  table.foreignId('song_id').constrained('song').cascadeOnDelete();
});
```

## Define it

Add a field with `@ManyToMany(...)` to each model that needs it.
The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

```dart title="lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

## Load it

The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways.
Use the field name (`'songs'`) as the relation name.

### `preload`

Use it when you load the models with a query.

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();
```

`preload` works with `find`, `get`, `all` and `getFirst`.
For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them.
A model without links gets an empty list.

### `$getRelation`

Use it when you already have the model.

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);
```

### `related`

Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];
```

It does not set `artist.songs`.
The query joins the pivot table, so write `table.column` for column names.

### `eager`

Use it when every query of `Artist` should load the relation.

```dart
@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

You do not call `preload`.
Do not set `eager: true` on both sides. Each side would load the other side again and again.

The load runs this SQL:

```sql
SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)
```

With `withPivot` or `withTimestamps`, it also selects those pivot columns, like `"artist_song"."role" as "_pivot_role"`.

`reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).

## Read pivot columns

The pivot table can have more columns, like a `role`.
List them in `withPivot`.
Read them with `pivot` on each related model.

```dart
@ManyToMany(Song, withPivot: <String>['role'])
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
for (Song song in artist!.songs) {
  print(song.pivot['role']);
}
```

- `pivot` has the two pivot keys, like `artist_id` and `song_id`, when the rows are loaded by the relation:
  with `preload`, `$getRelation`, `eager` or `related('songs')!.get()`.
  They are read from the loaded rows, so a relation without `withPivot` runs no extra SQL.
- `withTimestamps: true` adds `created_at` and `updated_at` to `pivot`.
  `attach()`, `sync()` and `toggle()` then set them.
  `updateExistingPivot()` sets `updated_at`.
  The pivot table needs both columns (`table.timestamps()`).
- A model that was not loaded by a ManyToMany relation has an empty `pivot`.
- `pivot` is not in `toJson()`. Read it in Dart and add it to your response yourself.

## Change the links

These methods add and remove rows in the pivot table.
The first argument is the relation name, like `'songs'`.
Save the model first. A model without an id throws a `StateError`.

The ids can be:

- one id: `1`
- a model: `song`
- a list of ids or models: `[1, 2, song]`
- a map of `id => pivot values`: `{1: {'role': 'singer'}, 2: {}}`

`null` means no ids. So `attach('songs', null)` and `detach('songs', null)` change nothing, and `sync('songs', null)` deletes every link, like `sync('songs', [])`.
Ids match with one rule:

- Two texts only match when the text is the same.
  So on a text key column, `'007'` and `'7'` are two ids.
  The ORM does not know the type of the key column, so `attach('songs', ['1', '01'])` adds two rows.
- When one id is a number (`int` or `double`), Dart reads the other one as a number.
  It trims the text, drops a `.0` end, and tries `int.tryParse` (`' 1'`, `'+1'`, `'01'`, `'1.0'`), then `double.tryParse` (`'1.'`, `'1e0'`).
  They match when the two numbers are the same.
  Rows of a number key column come back as numbers, so `sync('songs', ['01'])` keeps the row of song `1`.
- This is only how Dart matches ids. The databases read some texts in other ways.
  For example, `'0x1'` is `1` in Dart and on Postgres, `0` on MariaDB, and an error on MySQL.
  Postgres throws for `'1.0'`, `'1.'` and `'1e0'` on an integer column.
- A given text that only reads as a number at or past ±2^53, like `'1e20'` or `'9007199254740993.'`, is not exact.
  It throws an `ArgumentError` when it is matched to a number.
  `sync` checks every id before its first write.
- A stored value never throws. A value in the table that can not be read exactly does not match a number.
  So a long digit text in a text key column does not stop `sync`.
- A bool id is `1` or `0`, like the databases read it. So `sync('songs', true)` keeps the row of song `1`.
- A `BigInt` id is an `int` when it fits, else it throws an `ArgumentError`. Any other id type that is not an `int`, a `String`, a `bool`, a `double` or a model throws an `ArgumentError`.
- Each id finds its own stored row when it can. A row with the same text wins, so on a text key `1` finds `'1'`, not `'01'`.
  A stored row is matched once, so on a number key `toggle('songs', ['1', '01'])` detaches song `1` once.
- `detach` and `updateExistingPivot` send every given id.
  So on a text key, `detach('songs', [1, '01'])` deletes both rows.
- `sync` deletes a stored row only when none of the given ids matches it.
  So on a text key, `sync('songs', [1, '01'])` keeps the rows `'1'` and `'01'`.
- A new row is added once for ids that are the same by this rule, and the first id wins.
  So on a number key `attach('songs', [1, '01'])` adds one row. On a text key it adds only the row `1`.
- A whole double within ±2^53, like `2.0`, is sent as the int `2`.
  Any other double, like `1.5`, NaN, infinity or `1e20`, throws an `ArgumentError`.
- Text ids are sent to the database as they are.

A `null` id or a model that is not saved is skipped by `attach`, `detach`, `toggle`, `syncWithoutDetaching` and `updateExistingPivot`.
`sync` throws an `ArgumentError` for one, before it changes anything, because it would delete every other link.
Each id is used once: `[1, 1, '1']` adds one row.

A text key column can compare text without case.
This is the default in MySQL and MariaDB, and in SQLite with `COLLATE NOCASE`.
`COLLATE NOCASE` ignores case only. MariaDB can also ignore end spaces.
Dart does not know that. So `sync` and `toggle` also ask the database about each text id that Dart did not match.
Dox asks the database about all of these ids in one query (one query per 100 ids), with `WHERE key = id` for each id.
When it finds a stored row, that row counts as a match. With a stored `'ABC'`:

- `sync('songs', ['abc'])` keeps the row `'ABC'`. It adds no row and deletes nothing.
- `toggle('songs', ['abc'])` detaches the row `'ABC'`. It adds no row.
- The delete never removes a row that the database sees as a kept id.
- `detached` has only the ids whose row is really gone.

### `attach`

Adds a pivot row for each id.
The third argument has the pivot values for every new row.

```dart
await artist.attach('songs', 1);
await artist.attach('songs', <int>[2, 3], <String, dynamic>{'role': 'singer'});
await artist.attach('songs', <int, Map<String, dynamic>>{
  4: <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'},
});
```

`attach` does not check for a row that is already there.
Use `sync` or `syncWithoutDetaching` when the row may be there.

### `detach`

Deletes the pivot rows of the ids.
With no ids argument, it deletes every pivot row of the model.
`detach('songs', null)` deletes nothing.
It returns how many rows it deleted.
The songs stay in the `song` table.

```dart
await artist.detach('songs', <int>[1, 2]);
await artist.detach('songs');
```

### `sync`

Makes the pivot rows match the ids.

- It adds a row for each new id.
- It deletes the rows of the ids that are not in the list.
- It sets the pivot values of the rows that are already there, when a value changed. `updated` has those ids.

It returns a `PivotSyncResult` with the ids of each change.
A number id is an `int` in the result, also when you gave `'3'`.
A text that is not the plain text of an int, like `'03'` or `'007'`, stays text.

```dart
PivotSyncResult result = await artist.sync('songs', <int>[1, 2, 3]);
print(result.attached); // ids that got a new row
print(result.detached); // ids whose row was deleted
print(result.updated);  // ids whose pivot values changed
```

`syncWithoutDetaching` does the same, but it does not delete rows.

```dart
await artist.syncWithoutDetaching('songs', <int>[4]);
```

### `toggle`

Adds a row for each id that has none.
Deletes the row of each id that has one.
It returns a `PivotSyncResult` with `attached` and `detached`.

```dart
await artist.toggle('songs', <int>[1, 2]);
```

### `updateExistingPivot`

Sets pivot values on the rows of one id or a list of ids.
It returns how many rows changed.

```dart
await artist.updateExistingPivot('songs', 1, <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'});
```

## Filter by it

`whereHas()` keeps the artists that have a song.
It checks the pivot table `artist_song` for you.
It does not load the songs.

```dart
List<Artist> artists = await Artist().whereHas('songs', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('title', 'Yesterday');
}).get();

List<Artist> noSongs = await Artist().whereDoesntHave('songs').get();
```

See [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

## Options

The examples are for `@ManyToMany(Song)` in the `Artist` model.

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pivotTable` | the two model names in A-Z order, joined with `_` | `artist_song` | The pivot table. |
| `pivotForeignKey` | `{this model}_id` | `artist_id` | The pivot column that points to this model. |
| `pivotRelatedForeignKey` | `{related model}_id` | `song_id` | The pivot column that points to the related model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | `id` | The column in `artist` that `pivotForeignKey` points to. |
| `relatedKey` | the primary key of the related model | `id` | The column in `song` that `pivotRelatedForeignKey` points to. |
| `withPivot` | none | `['role']` | Extra pivot columns to read. See [Read pivot columns](#read-pivot-columns). |
| `withTimestamps` | `false` | `true` | Read and set `created_at` and `updated_at` in the pivot table. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

The defaults use the class names in snake_case, not the table names.
So `@DoxModel(table: 'artists')` does not change them.

- `Artist` and `Song` give `artist_song`.
- `Blog` and `Category` give `blog_category`.
- `BlogPost` and `Tag` give `blog_post_tag`.

### Set all keys

```dart
@ManyToMany(
  Song,
  pivotTable: 'artist_song',
  pivotForeignKey: 'artist_id',
  pivotRelatedForeignKey: 'song_id',
  localKey: 'id',
  relatedKey: 'id',
)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

### `onQuery`

`onQuery` is a static function in the same model class.
It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

```dart
@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @ManyToMany(Song, onQuery: onlyPublished)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Song> onlyPublished(Song q) {
    return q.where('song.status', 'published');
  }
}
```

## In JSON

- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`.
- A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query.
- The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `songs`.


---

# Polymorphic

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/polymorphic/

# Polymorphic

Use a polymorphic relation when one model can belong to more than one other model.

For example, a comment can belong to a photo or to a video.
The `comment` table does not have a `photo_id` and a `video_id`.
It has two columns:

- `commentable_id`: the id of the photo or the video.
- `commentable_type`: the type, like `photo` or `video`.

`commentable` is the morph name. You pick it.

## Tables

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `photo` | `id`, `title` |
| `video` | `id`, `title` |
| `comment` | `id`, `body`, `commentable_id`, `commentable_type` |

`morphs()` adds both columns and an index:

```dart
await schema.create('comment', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('body');
  table.morphs('commentable');
  table.timestamps();
});
```

## The morph map

The morph map gives each model a type name.
The type name is the value in the `commentable_type` column.

Set it in the `setup()` of a [provider](../../../digging-deeper/providers.md).
Dox runs providers in every isolate, before the first request.
The map is kept per isolate, so setting it only in `main()` is not enough.
Then the other isolates store the class name, and `@MorphTo` throws there.

```dart
class MorphMapProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.morphMap(<String, Model<dynamic> Function()>{
      'photo': Photo.new,
      'video': Video.new,
    });
  }
}
```

A queue worker or a CLI command that reads these relations must call it too.

- `@MorphTo` needs it. It reads the type and makes the model from the map.
- Without a map, `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne` store the class name, like `Photo`.
- Use a morph map in production. The class name changes when you rename the class, or when you build with `--obfuscate`. Then the old rows do not match.
- Do not change a type name later. The rows in the table keep the old name.
- `Model.morphMap(map, merge: false)` removes the names you set before.

Two helpers read the map:

```dart
String type = Model.morphTypeOf(Photo()); // 'photo'
Model<dynamic> model = Model.morphModel('video'); // a new Video()
```

## Define it

### `@MorphMany`

A photo has many comments.
The second argument is the morph name.

```dart title="lib/app/models/photo/photo.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../comment/comment.model.dart';

part 'photo.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Photo extends PhotoGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable')
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}
```

### `@MorphOne`

A photo has one cover image.
It works like `@MorphMany`, but the field is one model.

```dart
@MorphOne(Image, 'imageable')
Image? cover;
```

When there are many rows, it keeps the last row the query returns.
Add an `orderBy` in `onQuery` to pick the row, like with [HasOne](has-one.md).

### `@MorphTo`

A comment belongs to a photo or a video.
The field type is `Model<dynamic>?`.
The morph name is the field name in snake_case: `commentable`.
The `commentable_id` and `commentable_type` columns must be `@Column` fields, or the relation is always `null`.

```dart title="lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? body;

  @Column()
  int? commentableId;

  @Column()
  String? commentableType;

  @MorphTo()
  Model<dynamic>? commentable;
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

## Save a row

There is no `associate()`. Set the two columns yourself.
Use `Model.morphTypeOf()` for the type, so it is the same as the morph map.

```dart
Comment comment = Comment()
  ..body = 'Nice'
  ..commentableId = photo.id
  ..commentableType = Model.morphTypeOf(photo);
await comment.save();
```

## Load it

Load it like the other relations: `preload`, `$getRelation`, `related` or `eager`.

```dart
Photo? photo = await Photo().preload('comments').find(1);
print(photo?.comments.length);

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('commentable').get();
for (Comment c in comments) {
  if (c.commentable is Photo) {
    print((c.commentable as Photo).title);
  }
}
```

- `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne` run one query for all models.
  It has `where commentable_type = 'photo'`.
- `@MorphTo` runs one query for each type in the list.
  A comment with a type that is not in the morph map throws a `StateError`.
  A comment with no type, or an empty type `''`, gets `null`.
- `related<Photo>('commentable')` on one comment gives the query of its photo.

`reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).

## Filter by it

`whereHas()`, `whereDoesntHave()` and `withCount()` work with `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne`.

```dart
List<Photo> photos = await Photo().whereHas('comments').get();
List<Video> videos = await Video().withCount('comments').get();
```

They do not work with `@MorphTo`. It throws an `UnsupportedError`.

## Options

### `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne`

The examples are for `@MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable')` in the `Photo` model.

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` (2nd argument) | | `commentable` | The morph name. |
| `typeColumn` | `{name}_type` | `commentable_type` | The type column in `comment`. |
| `idColumn` | `{name}_id` | `commentable_id` | The id column in `comment`. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | `id` | The column in `photo` that `idColumn` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

### `@MorphTo`

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | the field name in snake_case | `commentable` | The morph name. |
| `typeColumn` | `{name}_type` | `commentable_type` | The type column in this table. |
| `idColumn` | `{name}_id` | `commentable_id` | The id column in this table. |
| `ownerKey` | the primary key of the related model | `id` | The column in the related table that `idColumn` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query of each type. It runs for every type, so it takes and returns `Model<dynamic>`. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

## In JSON

- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`.
- A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query.
- The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `comments`, `commentable`.


---

# Authentication

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/authentication/

# Authentication

This page shows how to log users in with `dox_auth` and protect routes with a JWT token, an access token or a session.

`dox_auth` checks an email and a password against your user table.
It gives back a JWT token, or an [access token](#access-tokens) with `AccessTokenAuthDriver`.
The client sends this token in the `Authorization` header.
`AuthMiddleware` reads the token and loads the user from the database.

## Install

```bash
dart pub add dox_auth
```

A new app made with the `dox` CLI already has it.

## 1. Hide the password in the model

By default, the token holds the user data as JSON (`toJson()`), and anyone can read a JWT.
So the password hash must never be in `toJson()`.
Put it in `hidden`.
For a token that holds only the user id, see [Small tokens](#small-tokens).

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users')
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}
```

## 2. Set up the auth provider

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'web',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'web': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}
```

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run `dart run build_runner build` and it is in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.

## 3. Add the routes

`AuthMiddleware` protects a route.
When the token is missing or not valid, the request stops with `401 Authentication failed`.
Put these routes in `register()` of the `ApiRouter`. Its prefix is `api`, so the paths start with `/api`.
A [rate limit](rate-limiting.md) on login and register slows down password guessing.

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.get('/auth/user', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.user]);
```

## 4. Write the controller

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// Make an account and log in.
  Future<dynamic> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User();
    user.name = body.name;
    user.email = body.email;
    user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': user};
  }

  /// Check the email and password. Give a token.
  Future<dynamic> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// The logged in user.
  User? user(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }
}
```

`RegisterUser` and `LoginUser` are `@Dto` classes. See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md).

## 5. Send the token from the client

```http
GET /api/auth/user
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The `Bearer` prefix can be in any case, so `bearer <token>` also works.
`JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req)` gives the token of a request.

## Read the user

After `AuthMiddleware`, `req.auth` holds the login.

| Code | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `req.auth` | an `IAuth?`. `null` when the route has no `AuthMiddleware`. It is kept apart from the input, so a query or body field can not set it |
| `req.auth?.isLoggedIn()` | `true` when a user is loaded |
| `req.auth == null` | `true` for a guest |
| `req.auth?.id()` | the primary key of the user, or `null`. It works when the key is in `hidden` |
| `req.auth?.user<User>()` | the user model |
| `req.auth?.toJson()` | the user as a map, without `hidden` fields |

## The `Auth` class

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Auth.initialize(AuthConfig)` | sets the config. Call it once, in a provider |
| `Auth(guard: 'admin')` | uses another guard from `guards`. Without `guard`, it uses `defaultGuard` |
| `await Auth().attempt(credentials)` | finds the user and checks the password. Gives a token, or `null` |
| `Auth().login(user)` | gives a token for this user, with no password check |
| `Auth().setUser(req, user)` | sets this user on `req.auth`, with no token and no password check. For your own auth middleware |
| `Auth(ip: req.ip())` | gives the client ip to `attempt`, for the [login throttle](#login-throttle) |
| `await Auth().revokeToken(req)` | revokes the bearer token of this request (a JWT logout). Needs [revocation](#revoke-tokens) |
| `await Auth().revokeAllTokens(id)` | revokes all tokens of this user made before the current second. A token made in the same second still works. Needs [revocation](#revoke-tokens) |
| `await Auth().forgetUser(id)` | drops this user from the `userCacheTtl` cache. Needs [revocation](#revoke-tokens) |
| `Auth.needsRehash(hash)` | `true` when the hash was not made with the cost of `Hash.rounds`. See [Password hash cost](#password-hash-cost) |
| `Auth.hashCost(hash)` | the bcrypt cost of a hash, or `null` when it is not a bcrypt hash |
| `user<T>()` | the user after `attempt` or `login` |
| `await Auth().once(credentials)` | checks the password like `attempt`. Gives `true` or `false`. It makes no token and does not touch the session. The user is logged in for this `Auth` only |
| `isLoggedIn()` | `true` when there is a user |
| `check()` | the same as `isLoggedIn()` |
| `guest()` | `true` when there is no user |
| `id()` | the primary key of the user, or `null` for a guest |

`attempt` searches only by the fields in `identifierFields`. It runs bcrypt also when no user is found, or when the user has no password, so the answer time does not tell whether an email has an account.
It returns `null` when the password is not a `String`, when no identifier is given, when an identifier is not a string or a number (a map or a list from the body), or when the password does not match.

## Options

### `AuthProvider`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | required | a function that makes a new model, like `() => User()` |
| `identifierFields` | `['email']` | the fields `attempt` searches by |
| `passwordField` | `'password'` | the column with the bcrypt hash |

### `JwtAuthDriver`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `secret` | required | the key that signs tokens, like `SecretKey(env.appKey)`. An empty key throws `ArgumentError`. A key shorter than 32 bytes also throws in production, and prints a warning in development, local, test and testing. Make one with `dox key:generate`. For a separate JWT secret (not `APP_KEY`), `openssl rand -hex 32` also works. Dox does not sign with this text as it is: the HMAC key is made from it with HKDF-SHA256 and the label `dox:jwt`. Another service that checks the tokens needs that key: `driver.signingKey` |
| `algorithm` | `JWTAlgorithm.HS256` | the signing algorithm. A token with another algorithm in its header is rejected |
| `expiresIn` | `Duration(hours: 1)` | how long a token is valid |
| `issuer` | `null` | the `iss` claim. When set, `verifyToken` also checks it |
| `hashRounds` | `10` | the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes. Use the same value as `Hash.rounds` |
| `userCacheTtl` | `null` (off) | keep the user of a token in memory for this time. See below |
| `previousSecrets` | `null` | old secrets, only to check tokens after a key change. `null` with `secret` = `APP_KEY`: the old keys come from `AppConfig.previousKeys`. `[]` turns it off. See below |
| `minimalPayload` | `false` | put only the user id (the `sub` claim) in new tokens. See [Small tokens](#small-tokens) |
| `revocation` | `false` | turn on token revocation. See [Revoke tokens](#revoke-tokens) |
| `revocationStore` | `null` | the cache store for revoked tokens. `null` is the default app store |

### Change the JWT secret

New tokens are always signed with `secret`.
A token is checked with `secret` first, then with each old secret.
Only a wrong signature moves on to the next secret. An expired token fails at once.

- **The secret is `APP_KEY`** (`SecretKey(env.appKey)`): follow [Change the key](encryption.md#change-the-key-key-rotation). The old keys in `AppConfig.previousKeys` are used. You need nothing more.
- **A separate JWT secret**: give the old one to the driver.

    ```dart
    JwtAuthDriver(
      secret: SecretKey(env.jwtSecret),
      previousSecrets: <JWTKey>[SecretKey(env.jwtOldSecret)],
    )
    ```

Remove the old secret once `expiresIn` has passed. Then every old token has expired anyway.
Do not keep a leaked secret: anyone who has it can make tokens.

### Small tokens

By default, a token holds the user (`toJson()`, `hidden` fields left out), plus the `iat`, `exp` and `jti` claims.
Anyone can read a JWT payload.
The safer choice is a small token:

```dart
JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey), minimalPayload: true)
```

The token then holds only the user id (the `sub` claim).
Load the user with `req.auth?.user<User>()`, not from the token.
A front end that reads user fields from the token must then get the user from the API.

## Revoke tokens

By default, a token works until it expires. There is no server list of tokens.
Turn on revocation to stop a token before it expires:

```dart
JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
  revocation: true,
  revocationStore: 'auth',
)
```

Each token has a random id (the `jti` claim).
With revocation on, the JWT driver keeps revoked tokens in the app cache (`Cache()` of `dox_core`).
A revoked token stops working at once:

```dart
await Auth().revokeToken(req);     // revoke the bearer token of this request (a JWT logout)
await Auth().revokeAllTokens(id);  // revoke all tokens of a user, eg. after a password change or a ban
await Auth().forgetUser(id);       // drop the user from `userCacheTtl`, eg. after a ban
```

- With revocation off, these three methods throw a `StateError`. So no one thinks a token is revoked when it is not.
- With revocation off, `verifyToken` never reads the cache.
- `Auth().logout(req)` is the session logout. For a JWT, use `revokeToken`.
- A revoked token stays on the deny-list only until it expires.
- `revokeAllTokens` keeps tokens made after the call. A token made in the same second as the call also still works.
- A token with no `jti` claim can not go on the deny-list, so `revokeToken` does nothing for it. `revokeAllTokens` still stops it when it has an `iat` claim. Tokens from `JwtAuthDriver` have one.
- The `revokeAllTokens` time comes from the server clock. Keep server clocks in sync (NTP).
- Give auth its own store, and never flush it. For example, a `redis` store with its own prefix. A flush of this store (`Cache().flush()`), or a `memory` store with `max_size` that drops old keys, brings revoked tokens back until they expire.
- Cost: `verifyToken` reads this store on every request, also with `userCacheTtl`. It is one `many()` call: one round trip on `redis` and `memory`. On the `file` store (the default) it is 2 or 3 file reads per request. Use `memory` for one isolate, or `redis` for many isolates or servers.
- When the store can not be read, the token is checked with only the signature and `exp`, and a warning is printed once. So a cache outage does not log everyone out. But revoked tokens work until the store is back.

## Access tokens

Access tokens are API tokens that you can revoke at any time.
They are like AdonisJS access tokens or Laravel Sanctum tokens.
They are opt-in. Session and JWT guards do not change.

A token looks like `oat_12.<secret>`.
The table keeps only a SHA-256 hash of the secret.
You see the plain token once, when you make it.
A token works until it expires or you revoke it.

### 1. Add the guard

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
'api': AuthGuard(
  driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(), // table: 'auth_access_tokens', expiresIn: null (no end)
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),
```

`AccessTokenAuthDriver` options:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `table` | `'auth_access_tokens'` | The table of the tokens. |
| `connection` | the default connection | The `dox_orm` connection name. |
| `expiresIn` | `null` (no end) | How long a new token works. |
| `hashRounds` | `10` | The bcrypt cost, for `attempt`. |
| `type` | the guard name | The type of the tokens. A token works only on a guard with the same type. |
| `stringIds` | `false` | `true` for users with text ids. Text ids are compared exactly. Use the same value in the migration. For uuid ids, see `uuidIds`. |
| `uuidIds` | `false` | `true` for users with uuid ids. A uuid is kept and compared in lower case. Use the same value in the migration. |

### 2. Add the table

Run `dox auth:tokens-table`. It writes a migration in `db/migration` that makes the `auth_access_tokens` table. Then run `dox migrate`.

```bash
dox auth:tokens-table
dox migrate
```

`auth:tokens-table` is a [package command](../digging-deeper/package-commands.md) of `dox_auth`. It does not overwrite: when a `create_access_tokens_table` migration is already there, it prints so and stops.

Flags:

- `--uuid`: for users with uuid ids (`uuidIds: true`).
- `--string-ids`: for users with text ids (`stringIds: true`).
- `--users-table=users`: adds a foreign key to this table (`usersTable:`).
- `--users-key=uid`: the key column of the users table, when it is not `id` (`usersKey:`).

For other options, like `table:`, edit the migration file. The migration it writes looks like this. You can also write it by hand. `AccessTokenTables` makes the table.

```dart title="db/migration/2026_11_02_000000000_create_access_tokens_table.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

/// The auth_access_tokens table of dox_auth.
class CreateAccessTokensTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await AccessTokenTables.up(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await AccessTokenTables.down(schema);
  }
}
```

`AccessTokenTables.up` options:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `table` | `'auth_access_tokens'` | The table name. Use the same name as the driver `table`. |
| `stringIds` | `false` | `false`: `tokenable_id` is an unsigned big int, like Sanctum and AdonisJS. `true`: it is text, for users with text ids. Use the same value as the driver `stringIds`. For uuid ids, see `uuidIds`. |
| `uuidIds` | `false` | `true`: `tokenable_id` is a uuid column (`UUID` on Postgres), for users with uuid ids. Then `usersTable` works with a uuid id. Set `uuidIds: true` on the driver too. |
| `usersTable` | none | Adds a foreign key from `tokenable_id` to `usersKey` of this table, with cascade delete. Then the tokens of a deleted user are deleted too. The two id columns must have the same type. |
| `usersKey` | `'id'` | The key column of `usersTable`, for the foreign key. |

With `usersTable`, use one token table per user model. If you have more than one user model (like users and admins), give each model its own token table, with `table:` on the driver and in the migration. With one shared table, the foreign key fails for admin tokens, and deleting a user also deletes the tokens of the admin with the same id.

The migration makes the table on the default connection.
If the driver uses another connection, like `AccessTokenAuthDriver(connection: 'other')`, make the table on that connection.

The table has these columns: `id`, `tokenable_type`, `tokenable_id`, `type`, `name`, `hash`, `abilities`, `last_used_at`, `expires_at`, `created_at`, `updated_at`.

### 3. Make and revoke tokens

```dart
// log in with a password: a new token with all abilities, or null
String? token = await Auth(guard: 'api').attempt(credentials);

// or make a token for a user
AccessToken token = await Auth(guard: 'api').createAccessToken(
  user,
  name: 'cli', // at most 255 characters
  abilities: <String>['posts:read'], // default: ['*'] (all)
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30), // default: the driver expiresIn
);
return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value}; // shown only once

await Auth(guard: 'api').accessTokens(user);           // all tokens of the user, newest first
await Auth(guard: 'api').revokeAccessToken(user, id);  // false when the user has no such token
await Auth(guard: 'api').revokeAllAccessTokens(user);  // eg. after a password change
await Auth(guard: 'api').revokeToken(req);             // logout: revoke the token of this request
await Auth(guard: 'api').pruneExpiredAccessTokens();   // delete expired tokens, eg. from a scheduled job
```

In a route behind `AuthMiddleware`, `(req.auth as Auth).revokeToken(req)` uses the token that was already checked. So it does not check the token again.

`accessTokens` gives `AccessToken` objects. `token.toJson()` has no hash and no plain token, so you can send it to the client.

### 4. Protect routes and check abilities

The client sends `Authorization: Bearer oat_12.<secret>`.
Protect the route with `AuthMiddleware(guard: 'api')`.
Then check the abilities of the token:

```dart
Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
if (!auth.tokenCan('posts:write')) {
  throw ForbiddenHttpException();
}
auth.currentAccessToken; // the AccessToken of this request
```

- A token fails (401) when its format is bad, the secret is wrong, it is expired, it was revoked, its user is gone, it has another type, or it was made for a guard with another user table.
- `tokenable_type` is the table name of the user model. If you rename the users table, the old tokens stop working.
- A revoked token is deleted from the table, so it stops working at once.
- A database error also fails the check (401). The error goes to `AppConfig.exceptionHandler`.
- Each token has a `type`. By default it is the guard name. So two access token guards do not take each other's tokens. If you rename a guard, set `AccessTokenAuthDriver(type: 'old-name')` to keep its tokens working.
- A token `name` over 255 characters throws an `ArgumentError`. Nothing is written.
- Pass a user of the guard's model. For admins, use `Auth(guard: 'admin').createAccessToken(admin)`. A user of another model throws an `ArgumentError`.
- On Postgres a uuid is stored in lower case. With `uuidIds`, the driver keeps and compares uuids in lower case too. On other databases, keep uuids in lower case in the users table.
- When you delete a user, call `revokeAllAccessTokens(user)` too, or use `usersTable` in the migration. Then old tokens can never match a new user with the same id.
- `tokenCan` is `false` when there is no access token. So a session or JWT login never passes it.
- `last_used_at` is written at most once a minute per token. So a busy token does not write on every request. If this write fails, the error is reported and the request goes on.
- `Auth().login(user)` throws a `StateError` with this driver. Use `createAccessToken`.
- Expired tokens stay in the table until you call `pruneExpiredAccessTokens()`.
- To check a token without a request, like in Socket.IO, use `Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token)`. See [Check a login with no request](#check-a-login-with-no-request). The driver method behind it is `check(token, guard)`, an instance method of `AccessTokenAuthDriver`.

## Login throttle

The login throttle limits failed logins per account and ip. It is off by default.
Turn it on in `register()` or `boot()` of a provider.
`Auth.throttle` is static, so each isolate has its own copy. If you set it in `main()` before the server starts, only the first isolate throttles.

```dart
Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle(maxAttempts: 5, decay: Duration(minutes: 1));

// JWT: pass the client ip
String? token = await Auth(ip: req.ip()).attempt(credentials);

// session: the ip comes from the request
bool ok = await Auth().attemptSession(req, credentials);
```

- After `maxAttempts` failed logins for the same login field (eg. the email) and ip, the next try throws `LoginThrottledException` (429) until `decay` has passed. Its `retryAfter` says how long to wait.
- A good login clears the count. The login field is trimmed and lower case, so `A@x.com` and `a@x.com` share one count.
- The counts live in the app cache. Pick a store with `LoginThrottle(store: 'redis')`. Use a shared store like `redis` for many isolates or servers.
- Without an ip, `attempt` counts per account only. Then anyone can lock an account for `decay`. So pass the ip.
- `attemptSession` sends a `Retry-After` header with the 429. `attempt` has no request, so catch `LoginThrottledException` and set the header from `retryAfter` if you need it.
- A burst of parallel tries can get a few more than `maxAttempts`, because the check and the count are separate cache steps.

## Password hash cost

Passwords use bcrypt with cost 10 by default. Each step up doubles the time of a login.
To raise it, set the cost for new hashes and tell the driver.
Then a login for an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password:

```dart
Hash.rounds = 12;
JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey), hashRounds: 12);
SessionAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);
```

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still work. Hash them again on the next good login:

```dart
if (Auth.needsRehash(user.password!)) {
  user.password = Hash.make(password);
  await user.save();
}
```

`Auth.needsRehash(hash, rounds: 12)` checks against another cost.

## More than one guard

Each guard has its own driver and its own user model.
For example, users and admins in two tables:

```dart
AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'admin': AuthGuard(
      driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => Admin()),
    ),
  },
);
```

Pick the guard by name:

```dart
String? token = await Auth(guard: 'admin').attempt(credentials);

Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin'), (AdminController c) => c.index]);
```

The token keeps the guard name in its `aud` claim.
So a token from the `web` guard does not work on the `admin` guard, even with the same secret.
An unknown guard name throws an `ArgumentError`.

## Custom guard (API key)

You can check the user in your own way, like an API key in the header.
Write a driver: extend `AuthDriver` and return the user from `verifyToken`.
`AuthMiddleware` and `req.auth` then work as with the other drivers.

The table stores a SHA-256 hash of each key in an `api_key_hash` column, not the key itself.
So a leak of the table does not leak the keys.
The example uses the `crypto` package (`dart pub add crypto`).

```dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:crypto/crypto.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` gives the user with this key.
class ApiKeyAuthDriver extends AuthDriver {
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> verifyToken(IDoxRequest req, String guard) async {
    String header = req.header('Authorization') ?? '';
    if (!header.startsWith('Bearer ')) return null;
    String key = header.substring(7).trim();
    String hash = sha256.convert(utf8.encode(key)).toString();
    Model<dynamic> model = AuthEngine().guard(guard).provider.model();
    return await model.where('api_key_hash', hash).getFirst();
  }

  /// no password login for this guard
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> attempt(Map<String, dynamic> credentials, String guard) async => null;

  /// no token to make: the key is the token
  @override
  String? createToken(Map<String, dynamic>? userPayload, String guard) => null;
}
```

Add it as a guard, and use the guard in the route:

```dart
'api': AuthGuard(
  driver: ApiKeyAuthDriver(),
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),

Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'api'), (DoxRequest req) => req.auth?.user<User>()]);
```

Make each key long and random, like `openssl rand -hex 32`. Then a fast hash like SHA-256 is safe. Do not use bcrypt here: you can not search by a bcrypt hash.

If you already have your own middleware, set the user with `Auth().setUser(req, user)`.
It needs no token and no password check. `req.auth` then gives this user:

```dart
User? user = await keys.userForKey(key);
if (user == null) throw UnAuthorizedException();
Auth(guard: 'api').setUser(req, user);
return req;
```

## Session login for web pages

For web pages, keep the login in the session instead of a token.
The browser sends the session cookie, so the client does nothing.
It needs `SessionMiddleware` and `CsrfMiddleware`. See [Session](../the-basic/session.md).

Use `SessionAuthDriver` in the guard:

```dart
'web': AuthGuard(
  driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),
```

Log in and log out with the request:

```dart
Future<dynamic> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
  bool ok = await Auth().attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{
    'email': body.email,
    'password': body.password,
  });
  if (!ok) {
    req.session.flashErrors(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'Wrong email or password'});
    return back(req);
  }
  return redirect('/dashboard');
}

DoxResponse logout(DoxRequest req) {
  Auth().logout(req);
  return redirect('/');
}
```

Send guests to the login page instead of a `401`:

```dart
Route.get('/dashboard', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login'), (PageController c) => c.dashboard]);
```

A public page can still know the user. `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)` sets `req.auth` when the login is good, and lets guests through too.
A guest, or a bad or expired token, goes on with `req.auth` as `null`.
With the JWT and access-token drivers, a database error also goes on as a guest, and it is reported.
With the session driver, a database error is not caught, so the answer is `500`.
`redirectTo` is ignored when `optional: true`.

Login and register pages are for guests only. `GuestMiddleware` lets only guests through.
A logged-in user goes to `redirectTo`. With no `redirectTo`, the answer is `403` with the code `already_logged_in`.

```dart
Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), (PostController c) => c.index]);
Route.get('/login', <dynamic>[GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard'), (PageController c) => c.login]);
```

Both take `guard:`, like `AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin')`.

`AuthMiddleware` also takes `guards:`, a list of guard names, like Laravel `auth:web,api`. It tries the guards in order. The first guard with a good login sets `req.auth`.

```dart
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']), (UserController c) => c.me]);
```

Set `guard:` or `guards:`, not both. Both, or an empty list, throws an `ArgumentError`.

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `await Auth().attemptSession(req, credentials)` | checks the password like `attempt`, and keeps the user id in the session. Gives `true` or `false` |
| `Auth().loginSession(req, user)` | keeps this user in the session, with no password check |
| `Auth().logout(req)` | removes the login and all session data. For a JWT, use [`revokeToken`](#revoke-tokens) |

- Login and logout give the session a new id and a new CSRF token. So an id that someone saw before the login is of no use.
- With the default `cookie` session driver, all session data sits in the cookie. So an old copy of the cookie still works after logout, until the session `lifetime` ends. If logout must really end old cookies, use the `cache` session driver, like `SessionConfig(driver: 'cache', store: 'redis')`.
- The session keeps only the user id. `AuthMiddleware` loads the user from the database on each request, so a deleted user is logged out.
- These methods throw a `StateError` on a guard that does not use `SessionAuthDriver`.
- `SessionAuthDriver` has one option, `hashRounds` (default `10`), like `JwtAuthDriver`.

## Check a login with no request

Code that has no request, like a [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) login, can check a token or a session itself:

```dart
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token);
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'web').userFromSession(session);
```

- `userFromToken` runs the same checks as a request with a `Bearer` header. For a JWT: signature, algorithm, guard, `exp` and [revocation](#revoke-tokens). For an [access token](#access-tokens): the hash, the type, the user table, `expires_at` and revocation. Give the token with no `Bearer ` prefix. A missing, bad, expired, revoked or changed token gives `null`. It needs a guard with `JwtAuthDriver` or `AccessTokenAuthDriver`.
- With an access token, `currentAccessToken` and `tokenCan` work on the same `Auth` after `userFromToken`.
- `userCacheTtl` is a cache, not a check. With it on, a deleted or banned user can still connect until the cache time ends, unless `forgetUser` runs.
- `userFromSession` gives the user of a session, or `null`. Load the session with `SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value)`. See [Session](../the-basic/session.md#load-a-session-with-no-request). It needs a guard with `SessionAuthDriver`.
- Both throw a `StateError` on a guard with the wrong driver.

## Things to know

- **The token is not secret.** By default, anyone with the token can read `user.toJson()`. Keep private columns in `hidden`, or use [small tokens](#small-tokens).
- **By default, you can not cancel one token.** A token works until it expires. Turn on [revocation](#revoke-tokens) to cancel one token, or all tokens of a user. Without revocation, to end all tokens, change the `secret` (your `APP_KEY`) with no old secrets. See [Change the JWT secret](#change-the-jwt-secret). Or use [access tokens](#access-tokens): they live in a table, and you can revoke them at any time.
- **The user is loaded on each request**, by the id in the token. A deleted user can not log in, even with a valid token.
- **`userCacheTtl` skips that query.** With `Duration(seconds: 30)`, a deleted or changed user is seen only after 30 seconds. Each isolate has its own cache. Requests in that time share one user object, so do not change it per request.
- **Login does not block the server.** `attempt` runs bcrypt in another isolate.
- **Hash passwords** before you save them. See [Hashing](hashing.md).


---

# Authorization

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/authorization/

# Authorization

This page shows how to say what a user may do, with gates and policies from `dox_auth`.

[Authentication](authentication.md) says who the user is.
Authorization says what this user may do.
For example, a user may edit their own post, but not the post of another user.

There are two ways to write the rules:

- A **gate** is one rule, written as a function.
- A **policy** is a class with all the rules of one model, like `Post`.

## Register the rules

Gates and policies are kept per isolate.
Dox runs many isolates, so add them in a provider.
The `setup()` of a provider runs in every isolate.

```dart title="lib/providers/gate_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/policies/post_policy.dart';

class GateProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
  }
}
```

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run `dart run build_runner build` and it is in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.

## Gates

A gate gets the user and a subject. It gives `true` when the user may do it.
The user and subject types come from the function.
A check with another type is denied.

```dart
Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
```

A gate with no subject uses `_` for the second parameter:

```dart
Gate.define('create-post', (User user, _) => user.verified == true);
```

A gate can be async:

```dart
Gate.define('publish-post', (User user, Post post) async {
  return await user.canPublishIn(post.categoryId);
});
```

### Check a gate

```dart
if (await Gate.allows(user, 'update-post', post)) {
  // the user may update the post
}

if (await Gate.denies(user, 'create-post')) {
  // the user may not create a post
}

// stop the request with 403 when denied
await Gate.authorize(user, 'update-post', post);

// true when the user may do at least one, or all of them
await Gate.any(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
await Gate.all(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
```

An ability with no gate and no policy is denied.

### Give a reason

A check can give a `GateResponse` instead of a `bool`.
The reason of `GateResponse.deny` is the message of the 403 answer.

```dart
Gate.define('delete-post', (User user, Post post) {
  if (post.published == true) {
    return GateResponse.deny('You can not delete a published post.');
  }
  return post.userId == user.id;
});

GateResponse response = await Gate.inspect(user, 'delete-post', post);
print(response.allowed);
print(response.message);
```

## Policies

A policy holds the rules of one model.
Write one method per ability.
A method takes the user, and the model when the ability needs one.
List the methods in `abilities`.

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    'create': create,
    'update': update,
    'delete': delete,
  };
}
```

Add the policy for its model:

```dart
Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
```

A check with a `Post` as the subject now uses the policy.
For an ability with no model, like `create`, pass the type `Post`:

```dart
await Gate.allows(user, 'update', post);
await Gate.allows(user, 'create', Post);
await Gate.authorize(user, 'delete', post);
```

Each method must take `(User user)` or `(User user, Post post)`.
A method with another signature fails at `Gate.policy`, so you see the mistake when the app starts.

When the policy has no method with the ability name, the gate with that name is used.

!!! note "Why a map of methods"
    Dart has no runtime reflection in compiled apps.
    So Dox can not find a method by its name.
    The `abilities` map links each name to its method.
    The methods stay normal typed Dart methods, so you can also call them directly in a test.

## In a controller

`req.can`, `req.cannot` and `req.authorize` use the logged-in user of `req.auth`.
Use them after `AuthMiddleware`.

```dart
Future<Post> update(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  await req.authorize('update', post);
  post.title = req.input('title');
  await post.save();
  return post;
}

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> show(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'post': post,
    'can_edit': await req.can('update', post),
  };
}
```

`req.authorize` answers `401` for a guest and `403` for a user who may not do it.

## On a route

The `Can` middleware checks an ability before the controller runs.
Put it after `AuthMiddleware`.

```dart
// a gate with no subject
Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('view-admin'), adminController.index]);

// a policy method with no model
Route.post('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('create', subject: Post), postController.store]);

// a policy method with the model of the route param
Route.bind<Post>('post', (String id) => Post().find(id));
Route.put('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('update', param: 'post'), postController.update]);
```

With `param`, the subject is the value of `Route.bind` for that route param.
When `Route.bind` finds nothing, the answer is `404`.

The answers:

- A guest who may not do it gets `401`.
- A logged-in user who may not do it gets `403`.

## Guests

A guest has no user. The user is `null`.
A gate or a policy is denied for a guest, unless its user type is nullable:

```dart
Gate.define('view-post', (User? user, Post post) {
  return post.published == true || post.userId == user?.id;
});

class CommentPolicy extends Policy<User?, Comment> {
  bool view(User? user, Comment comment) => comment.visible == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{'view': view};
}
```

`Can('view-post', param: 'post')` without `AuthMiddleware` then works for guests too.
But then a logged-in user is a guest too, because nothing loads the user.
Use `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)` on a public route. It loads the user when the login is good, and lets guests through:

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), Can('view-post', param: 'post'), postController.show]);
```

`req.can()` then also sees the user on a public route.

## Before and after hooks

`Gate.before` runs before every check.
It gives `true` or `false` to decide at once, or `null` to go on with the normal check.
For example, an admin may do anything:

```dart
Gate.before((User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null);
```

A hook runs only for users of its type. A `User` hook does not run for guests.

`Gate.after` sees the answer of every check, for example to log it.
It can not change the answer.

```dart
Gate.after((User user, String ability, GateResponse response) {
  print('${user.id} $ability ${response.allowed}');
});
```

A policy can have its own `before`. It runs before the methods of that policy:

```dart
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  @override
  bool? before(User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null;

  // ...
}
```

## In tests

`Gate.flush()` removes all gates, policies and hooks.
Call it in `setUp` when each test adds its own rules.

# CORS

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/cors/

# CORS

This page shows how to let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from `https://my.app` to `https://api.my.app` by default.
The API must send CORS headers to allow it.
Dox adds these headers from `CORSConfig`.

## Set up

The config is in `lib/config/cors.dart`. Pass it to `AppConfig(cors: cors)`.
A new app has this file with `enabled: false`, so it sends no CORS headers.
Set `origin` to the URL of your front end, and set `enabled: true`.

```dart title="lib/config/cors.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);
```

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);
```

## Options

Each option sets one response header.
An option that is `null` sends no header. All options except `enabled` are `null` by default.
So with no `origin`, Dox sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, and the browser blocks pages on other domains.

| Option | Header | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | - | `true` adds the headers to every route. Default: `true` |
| `origin` | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | one origin, a `List<String>` of origins, or `'*'` for all. A text is sent as it is, so do not put many origins in one text |
| `methods` | `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | a `List<String>` or a text like `'GET,POST'`. `'*'` allows all |
| `headers` | `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | a `List<String>` or a text. `'*'` allows all |
| `exposeHeaders` | `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` | the response headers the page may read |
| `credentials` | `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` | `true` lets the browser send cookies |
| `maxAge` | `Access-Control-Max-Age` | how many seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer |

For `methods`, `headers` and `exposeHeaders`, a list is joined with commas.

## More than one origin

`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` accepts only one origin or `*`.
So when `origin` is a list, Dox checks the `Origin` header of the request:

- The origin is in the list: Dox sends back that one origin.
- The origin is not in the list: Dox sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header. The browser blocks the call.
- The list has `'*'`: Dox sends `*`.

With a list, Dox also sends `Vary: Origin`. This tells caches that the answer depends on the origin.

```dart
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);
```

!!! warning "`credentials` with `*`"
    Do not use `origin: '*'` with `credentials: true`.
    Dox then sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and the browser blocks every call that has cookies.
    When you need cookies, set `origin` to your real front-end URL, or to a list of URLs.
    A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users, so list only sites you trust.

## Preflight requests

Before some requests, the browser sends an `OPTIONS` request.
You do not need an `OPTIONS` route for this.
Dox answers it with `204 No Content` and the CORS headers.
It uses the CORS setting of the route that the browser asks about.

## Turn CORS on or off for some routes

`enabled` is the default for all routes.
Change it for a group of routes:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});
```

# CSRF protection

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/csrf/

# CSRF protection

Cross site request forgery (CSRF) is an attack.

Another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app.
The browser sends your session cookie with it, so the request looks real.

`CsrfMiddleware` stops it. Each session has a secret token. A request that changes data must send it back. Another site can not read the token, so it can not send it.

## Turn it on

It needs a session, so put it after `SessionMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Now every `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` request must send the token. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets `419` with `{"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}`.

`GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests are not checked. Do not change data in a `GET` route.

## Send the token

Dox reads the token from one of these places:

- the `_token` field of the body (not the query string: a url ends up in logs and in the `Referer` header)
- the `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header
- the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header

The token is `req.session.token`.
Do not put it in a URL. URLs are kept in logs and in the browser history.

### HTML forms

Put the token in a hidden field.
With [views](../the-basic/views.md#forms), `csrfField()` writes this field for you:

```html
<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  {{ csrfField() }}
  ...
</form>
```

`csrfToken()` gives only the token, for example for a `<meta>` tag.

### axios and Inertia

Dox also sets an `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the token. It is not `HttpOnly`, so page scripts can read it.
axios reads this cookie and sends it in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header by itself. Inertia uses axios, so it works with no code.

With `fetch`, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

```js
const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});
```

## Skip some paths

Routes that other servers call (webhooks) or token based APIs can not send the token. List them in `except`:

```dart
const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);
```

- A path that ends with `*` matches everything that starts with it: `/api/*` matches `/api/posts` and `/api/users/5`.
- Any other path must match exactly.

An excluded path is not checked and gets no `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie.
Only skip paths that do not use the session login. A webhook should check its own signature instead.

## After login

`req.session.regenerate()` also makes a new token. Dox sends the new `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the same response.


---

# Encryption

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/encryption/

# Encryption

This page shows how to encrypt and decrypt text with `Crypt` and `AESEncryptor`.

Dox uses `AESEncryptor` to encrypt cookies with your `APP_KEY`.
You can also call it yourself.

## Encrypt with the app key

`Crypt` uses the `APP_KEY` of the app. You do not pass the key.

```dart
String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');
String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5}); // any JSON value
Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);
```

- `decryptString` and `decrypt` also try the old keys in `AppConfig.previousKeys`.
- They throw `DecryptException` when the text was changed or made with another key.
- `Crypt.encryptString(v)` gives the same as `AESEncryptor.encode(v, appKey)`.

## Encrypt and decrypt with your own key

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String secret = env.appKey;

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'
```

- `encode` returns base64 text.
- The same text gives a different output each time.
- `decode` throws `DecryptException` when the text was changed, or the key is wrong. It is a `400 Bad Request` error.
- The AES key is not the secret itself. Dox makes a 32-byte key (AES-256) from the secret with HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869) and a label. The default label is `dox:encrypt`. Pick another one with `purpose:`, like `AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice')`. `decode` needs the same `purpose`.

Make a new 32-character `APP_KEY` with the CLI:

```bash
dox key:generate
```

It writes a random key of letters and digits to `APP_KEY` in `.env`.

## One key per purpose

Dox does not use `APP_KEY` as it is. It makes one key per purpose from it, with HKDF-SHA256 and a label:

| Label | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `dox:cookie` | encrypted cookies, and the `cookie` session driver |
| `dox:jwt` | the HMAC key of `JwtAuthDriver` (with a `SecretKey`) |
| `dox:encrypt` | `AESEncryptor` when you give no `purpose` |
| `dox:signed-url` | for signed URLs |

So a value made for one purpose can not be used for another one.
`KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label)` gives the 32-byte key of a label. Each isolate makes it once.

At startup Dox checks `APP_KEY`. When it is empty, not exactly 32 bytes, or an old public sample key, the app stops.
In `development`, `local`, `test` and `testing` it only prints a warning.

- Keep `APP_KEY` in `.env` or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.
- If you change `APP_KEY` with no `previousKeys`, old encrypted cookies and sessions can not be read any more, so every user is logged out. JWT tokens signed with it stop working too. See [Change the key](#change-the-key-key-rotation).

## Change the key (key rotation)

Change `APP_KEY` from time to time, or when someone who knew it leaves the team.
With `previousKeys`, users stay logged in while you change it.

### Steps

1. Copy the current `APP_KEY` to `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`.
2. Run `dox key:generate`. It writes a new `APP_KEY`. Now `.env` has both:

    ```bash title=".env"
    APP_KEY=the-new-32-character-app-key....
    APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=the-old-32-character-app-key....
    ```

3. Read it in the env class, and give it to `AppConfig`:

    ```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    ```

    ```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
    AppConfig(
      appKey: env.appKey,
      previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
    )
    ```

4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.
5. Wait until the old cookies have expired: the session `lifetime`, and the `maxAge` of your own cookies.
6. Remove the old key from `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` and deploy again.

`APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` can hold more than one key, comma separated. Dox tries them in order.

### What reads the old keys

| Value | With an old key |
| --- | --- |
| encrypted cookies (`req.cookie`) | read |
| `cookie` session driver | read |
| CSRF token | read (it is in the session) |
| JWT tokens of `JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey))` | checked. A JWT secret that is not `APP_KEY` needs its own `previousSecrets` option, see [Authentication](authentication.md#change-the-jwt-secret). |
| `Crypt.decryptString` and `Crypt.decrypt` | read |
| `AESEncryptor.decode` in your code | read only when you pass `previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys` |
| anything new | made with `APP_KEY` only |

Dox writes a cookie with the new key the next time it sends that cookie.
So a user who comes back during step 5 moves to the new key without noticing.

### When the key leaked

Do **not** put a leaked key in `previousKeys`.
Anyone who has it can still make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts.
Change `APP_KEY` with no `previousKeys`. Every user is logged out, and that is what you want.

## Cookies

`DoxCookie` encrypts its value with `APP_KEY` by default.
`req.cookie(key)` decrypts it.
To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, call `DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value)`. It returns `null` when the value was changed, was made with another key, or was made for another cookie name.

```dart
return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted
DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted
String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent
```

`req.cookie(key)` returns `null` when the cookie was changed, was made with another `APP_KEY`, or was made for another cookie name.
The cookie name is bound to the encrypted value, so a value can not be copied from one cookie to another.

## How it works

`AESEncryptor` uses AES-256-GCM. The work runs in Rust (in `dox_http_native`), with the AES instructions of the CPU. One cookie takes about 1–2 µs.

- Each message gets a new random 12-byte nonce.
- The output is base64 of `nonce + encrypted text + tag`.
- The 16-byte tag checks the message. If someone changes one byte, `decode` throws.
- `encode` and `decode` also take `associatedData`, a text like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but `decode` needs the same value. Cookies use the cookie name here.

To store passwords, do not encrypt them. Hash them. See [Hashing](hashing.md).

# Hashing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/hashing/

# Hashing

This page shows how to hash passwords with `Hash` and check them later.

A hash is one-way. You can not turn it back into the password.
`Hash` uses bcrypt with a new random salt each time. It is in `package:dox_core/dox_core.dart`.

## Hash a password

Hash the password before you save it.

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();
```

`makeAsync` runs bcrypt in another isolate. See [Without blocking the server](#without-blocking-the-server).

The result looks like `$2a$10$...`. It holds the salt, so you only store this one string.
The same password gives a different hash each time.

## Check a password

```dart
bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', user.password!);
```

`Hash.verify(password, hashedPassword)` returns `true` when the password matches. `Hash.check` is the same, with the Laravel name.
It returns `false` when the password does not match, or when `hashedPassword` is not a valid bcrypt hash (for example an empty string).

## Without blocking the server

`Hash.make` and `Hash.verify` block the request isolate while bcrypt runs.
In a request handler, use the async versions. They run bcrypt in another isolate.

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);
```

## Cost

`Hash.rounds` is the bcrypt cost for new hashes. The default is `10`. Each step up doubles the time.
The cost must be from 4 to 31. Do not go below 10.

```dart
Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call
```

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still verify.
If you change it, also set `hashRounds` on `JwtAuthDriver` or `SessionAuthDriver` to the same value.
Then a login with an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password. See [Authentication](authentication.md).

## Long passwords

bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes.
`Hash.make` and `Hash.makeAsync` throw an `ArgumentError` when the password is longer than 72 bytes (UTF-8).
The error text does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs.
`Hash.verify` returns `false` for such a password.

So limit the length in your DTO, like `@Length(min: 8, max: 72)`.
`@Length` counts characters, and a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes.
So a password with such letters can still be too long. Catch the error and answer `422`, or use a smaller `max`.

## Compare secrets

To check an API key or a token, use `Hash.equals(given, expected)`, not `==`.
`==` stops at the first wrong character, so the time can tell how much of the key was right.
`Hash.equals` takes the same time for every value of the same length.

```dart
bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '', Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));
```

## Store tokens

For a long random secret that you keep in the database (an API key, an access token), store only `Hash.sha256(token)`.
Find the row by the hash of what the client sends.
SHA-256 is fast and gives the same hash for the same input, so a unique index works on it.

```dart
String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();
```

Never use `Hash.sha256` for passwords. A password is short and can be guessed, so use `Hash.make` (bcrypt).

## With login

You do not need `Hash.verify` for normal login.
`Auth().attempt()` from `dox_auth` finds the user and checks the password with bcrypt.
See [Authentication](authentication.md).

## Things to know

- Never store or encrypt a plain password. Hash it.
- Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the model `hidden` list.
- bcrypt is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow too. Do not hash in a loop on hot paths.

# Rate limiting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/rate-limiting/

# Rate limiting

`RateLimit` is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

Use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots like to hammer.

## Limit a route

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1)),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
```

Each client (by ip) can now send 5 login requests per minute. The 6th request gets:

```text
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 42
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

{"code":"too_many_requests","message":"Too Many Requests"}
```

- `Retry-After` is the number of seconds until the client can try again.
- Every answer, also a normal one, has `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining`.
- The error goes through your `exceptionHandler` and `responseHandler`, like any other error. So it has the same JSON shape as your other errors.

The defaults are `max: 60` and `per: Duration(minutes: 1)`.

## Limit every route

Put it in `globalMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

## Count by user, not by ip

`key` picks who is counted. The default is `req.ip()`.
The key is any `String`. For example, count by user id after `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart
Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);
```

!!! warning "Use a key the client can not choose"
    Do not count by a raw header, like `req.header('X-Api-Key')`.
    A client can send a new value with each request and get a new count each time.
    Count by a value that you checked first, like the id of the logged in user.

!!! warning "Behind a proxy"
    Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, every request comes from the proxy ip.
    Then all clients share one count. Add the proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, so `req.ip()` is the real client ip.
    See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

## Two limits on the same key

Two `RateLimit` with the same `max` and `per` share one counter for the same key. Give each one a `name` to keep them apart:

```dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);
```

## Where the counts live

Where the counts are kept depends on the default [cache](../digging-deeper/cache.md) store:

- When the default cache store is **Redis**, the counts are in Redis. All isolates and all servers share them. Use this when you run more than one server.
- Else the counts are in the **main isolate**. All isolates of the server share them, so `max` holds for the whole server.
  The other isolates send each count to the main isolate and wait for the answer. This is one small message per limited request.
  Each server has its own counts, so with 3 servers a client can send up to 3 x `max` requests.
  This is also true for the default `file` store of a new app.

To use one store by name, pass `store`:

```dart
RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')
```

A `memory` store named in `store` counts in the main isolate too. A store passed in `cacheStore` is used as it is.

## How it counts

It is a fixed window. With `per: Duration(minutes: 1)` the count starts at 0 at the start of each minute.
So a client can send `max` requests at the end of one minute and `max` more at the start of the next.
That is fine for most apps. For a hard limit, use a smaller window.

## See also

- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md)
- [Security headers](security-headers.md)
- [Production checklist](../reference/production-checklist.md)
